**The X-76 carries two kinds of engine so that no one machine has to both lift it and push it fast.** Two turboshafts lift it, a turbofan pushes it, and between those two modes its proprotors stop, fold and disappear \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\] \[[The War Zone on the X-76][ref_twz_x76]\]. **Every engineering number this article can derive about the aeroplane follows from that division**, and the most useful of them is that the turbofan's certificated thrust sets a ceiling on how much drag the aircraft may carry at 400 knots, a ceiling that under the simplest model of how thrust falls with altitude is the same at every altitude, a result derived in The Jet Is a Drag Budget.

The X-76A designation was allocated on 20 October 2025 to Bell Textron for the Speed and Runway Independent Technologies programme, SPRINT, of the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, which is DARPA. Its row has an engine cell reading `2 GE CT7-8, PW308C+`, a sponsor cell reading DARPA, and a description that the register marks as its compiler's wording rather than as drawn from Department of Defense records \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. The register is a compilation by Andreas Parsch published at designation-systems.net and not a Department of Defense publication.

> Unmanned demonstrator for *SPRINT* (Speed and Runway Independent Technologies) program.

**At this article's date of 15 December 2025 that row was not public.** It first appears in an archived copy of the register between 15 January and 1 February 2026 \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, as archived on 15 January 2026][ref_mds_addendum_wb_2026_01]\] \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, as archived on 1 February 2026][ref_mds_addendum_wb_2026_02]\], and DARPA announced the designation on 9 March 2026 \[[DARPA on the X-76][ref_darpa_x76]\]. **The programme behind it was public, and in unusual depth.** The solicitation of March 2023 is on the federal contracting portal with its proposers' day slides, three budget justification books inside the date carry a programme entry, the federal award record holds three of the four first-phase contracts, and Bell's patents describe stop-fold mechanisms of the kind the aircraft needs \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\] \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2024][ref_darpa_pb2024]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2025][ref_darpa_pb2025]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\] \[[Award HR001124C0325 to Aurora Flight Sciences][ref_award_aurora]\] \[[Award HR001124C0326 to Piasecki Aircraft][ref_award_piasecki]\] \[[Award HR001124C0327 to Northrop Grumman][ref_award_northrop]\] \[[US 10,526,068][ref_pat_us10526068]\]. **The article can therefore state the aeroplane's envelope from the government's documents and its engines from the register, and almost nothing else.** The designation itself, and the founding-year reading of its number, are treated in the [X-69 through X-75][related_post_a366_x69_through_x75_leapfrogged_block] article and are summarised here only where the aeroplane needs them.

**This article treats the X-76 as an aircraft and not as a designation alone**, because a vehicle exists and was being built after its critical design review. **It has not flown and will not fly inside the dateline**, so it is documentation-poor, and every section that would describe flight describes instead what the government asked for and what physics allows \[[DARPA on the X-76][ref_darpa_x76]\].

## The Research Question

**The programme states its question, and the solicitation and DARPA's programme page state it in the same numbers.** The solicitation asks for technologies that let an aircraft "cruise at speeds from 400 to 450 Knots, hover in austere environments, and transition between these modes of operation in a stable and time critical manner" \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. DARPA's programme page, as it stood on 12 December 2025, gives the same pair of numbers, cruise from 400 to 450 knots at relevant altitudes and hover in austere environments from unprepared surfaces \[[DARPA SPRINT programme page, as archived on 12 December 2025][ref_darpa_sprint_wb_2025_12]\].

**The question is therefore runway independence at jet cruise speed, a hard one because the two halves want opposite rotors.** Hover wants a large disk moving a large mass of air slowly, since the ideal power to hover falls as the square root of the disk area grows. High speed wants the opposite, a small, stiff propulsor whose blade tips stay subsonic when the aircraft's speed is added to their rotation. **A rotor big enough to hover efficiently is too big to cruise at 450 knots, and a propulsor fit for 450 knots is too small to hover efficiently.** Bell's 2025 paper states the same tension in one sentence, that hover requires significant power that can only be mitigated by larger diameter rotors, but that large diameter rotors become a detriment to achieving transonic flight \[[Schank et al. 2025][research_schank_xin_2025]\].

**Momentum theory states the hover half of that tension exactly.** An ideal rotor system of total disk area $A$ lifting a weight $W$ in air of density $\rho$ needs an induced power

$$
P_{\mathrm{ideal}} = \frac{W^{3/2}}{\sqrt{2 \rho A}},
\tag{1}
$$

so at fixed weight and density, doubling the disk area changes the ideal power by the factor

$$
\frac{P_{\mathrm{ideal}}(2A)}{P_{\mathrm{ideal}}(A)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 0.707,
\tag{2}
$$

a saving of 29 percent. The sizing section adds the figure of merit, the transmission loss and the wing download to this ideal, and quantifies the cruise half of the tension from the helical tip Mach number.

### Two Propulsion Systems, Each Sized by One Flight Phase

**The stop-fold answer is to stop asking one propulsor to do both jobs.** The proprotors lift the aircraft in hover and pull it through conversion like those of any tiltrotor. At some airspeed the wing carries the weight, a separate jet takes over the thrust, and the proprotors are feathered, stopped, and folded back along their nacelles. **The register's engine cell is the physical form of that answer**, two turboshafts and a turbofan. Engle and Sambell described the configuration in 1969 in terms that still fit, the rotors stopped in axial flow in a 120 to 200 knot range and the blades folded into streamlined pods, so that "the lift and propulsion systems can thus be optimized for their respective operating regimes" \[[Engle and Sambell 1969][research_engle_sambell_1969]\].

**This article's keystone is that sentence made quantitative.** If each system is sized by one phase, then the turboshafts' certificated power bounds what the aircraft can hover and the turbofan's certificated thrust bounds what it can push at 400 knots. Neither bound needs the aircraft's mass, wing or rotor diameter, which are not public, to be stated as an envelope. **Both envelopes are derived below**, and the most useful result is that the turbofan's sea-level rating, with an assumed lapse factor, fixes the largest equivalent drag area the aircraft can carry at 400 knots, at every altitude in the solicitation's band.

### Why a Proprotor Cannot Simply Be Driven Faster

**A conventional tiltrotor runs out of speed for two reasons that this article treats, and both are on the proprotor.** The first is aeroelastic. A large, flexible proprotor on a flexible wing can couple its gyroscopic precession to the wing's bending and torsion and go unstable, the instability called whirl flutter, and the speed at which it occurs falls as the wing is made thinner and less draggy \[[Acree et al. 1999][research_acree_johnson_1999]\] \[[Johnson 1974b][research_johnson_1974]\]. **The second is compressibility.** A blade tip sees the aircraft's forward speed and its own rotational speed combined, so the helical tip Mach number rises with airspeed even when the rotor turns no faster. A later subsection quantifies this second limit from the XV-15's published rotor speed. **The stop-fold configuration escapes both limits at once by removing the rotor from the airstream**, and a 1972 full-scale wind tunnel test reported that effect, the stopped rotor eliminating the rotor, pylon and wing instability \[[The History of the XV-15 Tilt Rotor Research Aircraft][ref_xv15_history]\].

**The research question, then, is not whether a rotor can be stopped in flight, which was shown at full scale in a wind tunnel in 1972.** It is whether an aircraft built around that idea, with existing engines and a flight control system that sequences the transition, can hover over an unprepared surface and then cruise at 400 knots, which no aircraft has done in the records this article consulted.

## The Register Row and Its Engine Cell

**The row has six cells and only the description is marked as the compiler's.** The date, the designation, the maker, the engines and the sponsor carry no mark and are, by the compiler's scheme, drawn from Department of Defense records, while the whole description cell carries the class the compiler uses for wording that is not from Department records \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **The engines are therefore the only configuration fact about this aeroplane in the public record that the compiler attributes to Department of Defense records**, and they are engines of two kinds, two turboshafts and, on the reading taken below, one turbofan.

**Two General Electric CT7-8 turboshafts are a helicopter powerplant.** The CT7-8 series is the commercial member of the family whose military members are the T700 engines, the New Zealand regulator's acceptance report recording that "the original CT7-1 turboshaft was a commercial derivative of the military T700 engine" \[[New Zealand type acceptance report for the CT7 series][ref_nz_ct7]\] and General Electric calling the line "the family of T700/CT7 turboshaft engines" \[[General Electric on the certification of new CT7-8 models, 2004][ref_ge_ct7_2004]\]. **In the copy of the register last updated on 23 August 2026, 23 other rows are powered by T700 or CT7 variants**, and 20 of them are helicopters, two are the HC-144 transports with turboprop CT7s, and one is the [X-49][related_post_a346_piasecki_x49], a compound helicopter \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **One PW308C is a business-jet turbofan** of about 31 kilonewtons \[[Type-certificate data sheet for the PW308 series][ref_easa_pw308]\], and the New Zealand regulator's acceptance report states that it "was developed for the Falcon 2000EX aircraft and is rated at 7002 lb. maximum takeoff thrust" \[[New Zealand type acceptance report for the PW308 series][ref_nz_pw308]\]. **The two documents agree to within a pound**, the European sheet's 31.15 kilonewtons being 7,003 pounds. **No other of its 539 rows pairs a turboshaft with a turbofan**, every other cell naming more than one kind of engine or thruster belonging to a missile, a target or a satellite, and that pairing is what a stop-fold aircraft is \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\].

### The Plus Sign After the Turbofan Has Four Readings

**The cell reads `2 GE CT7-8, PW308C+`, and the trailing plus sign is not explained anywhere in the register.** This article does not resolve it. It records the four readings that the evidence allows and the meaning of each.

**The first reading is that the plus is part of a model name, and the register supports it.** Two other rows end in a plus, the BQM-167A and the BQM-177A targets, both powered by a `Microturbo Tri 60-5+` \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\], and the Air Force's fact sheet for the first gives its power plant as "1 MicroTurbo Tri 60-5+", so in those rows the plus is part of the engine's name \[[Air Force BQM-167A fact sheet, as archived on 11 November 2025][ref_af_bqm167]\]. **Where the register combines two kinds of engine, a count and a second engine always follow the plus**, as in `1 XJ400-CA-400 + 1 Solid Propellant` and `1 Mark 104 Mod 3+ 1 Mark 72 Mod 1`, and in this row nothing follows it.

**The second reading is an improved PW308C.** Pratt and Whitney Canada announced an enhanced PW308C in June 2011 for the Falcon 2000S, with changes to the combustor and fuel delivery \[[AviTrader on the enhanced PW308C][ref_avitrader_pw308c]\]. **A compiler or a source document might mark that variant with a plus**, but none of the documents consulted does.

**The third reading is the solicitation's engine rule.** The solicitation requires existing engines and permits off-the-shelf engines with minor upgrades that make no change to the engine core \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\], and DARPA's answers to proposers say that "modifications that include the engine core are not allowed" \[[SPRINT questions and answers][ref_sprint_qa]\]. **A plus could mark such an upgrade.** That is an inference from the rule's existence and from nothing in the row.

**The fourth reading is truncation.** The plus could be the start of a combination whose second term was lost, an electrical machine or an auxiliary system for example. **The register's combination syntax makes this the least likely of the four**, since every combination it prints continues after the plus with a count and a name.

**Which engine count governs the turbofan is the same kind of question.** The count 2 precedes the CT7-8 and nothing precedes the PW308C. The register's other multi-type rows give a count for each type \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\], so **the cell, read literally, names two turboshafts and an unstated number of turbofans, and this article takes the turbofan count as one.** That reading agrees with the published renderings. DARPA's artist's concept, released on 9 March 2026 and so after the dateline, shows one lit exhaust at the tail between two canted fins, with the folded blades lying along each wingtip nacelle \[[DARPA artist's concept of the X-76][ref_darpa_x76_image]\], and a journalist's description of the renderings agrees \[[The Aviationist on the X-76][ref_aviationist_x76]\]. **An artist's concept is not an engineering drawing**, and the reading depends on the register cell first and the picture second. The count matters, because the certificated PW308C is approved for multiple-engine installation only \[[Type-certificate data sheet for the PW308 series][ref_easa_pw308]\], a point taken up under Dependent Systems.

### The Compiler's Description Calls It Unmanned

**The description calls the X-76 an unmanned demonstrator, and that word is not official.** The solicitation explicitly left crewing to the proposer, saying that "the decision to have the SPRINT X-Plane as manned, unmanned, optionally piloted, etc. is left to the proposer" \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. **Two documents inside the date are consistent with an uncrewed aircraft without saying so.** The solicitation's slides anticipate that "a flight termination system may be required if unmanned" \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\], and the fiscal year 2026 budget book plans "ground station and human-machine interface development" \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\]. **A ground station is what an uncrewed aircraft is flown from**, so the plans support the compiler's word, as an inference. After the date, DARPA released one rendering of the X-76 that shows no cockpit glazing \[[DARPA artist's concept of the X-76][ref_darpa_x76_image]\] and that journalists read as uncrewed and a second of a future operational aircraft described as optionally piloted \[[The War Zone on the X-76][ref_twz_x76]\] \[[DARPA SPRINT programme page][ref_darpa_sprint]\].

### The Row Was Not Public at This Article's Date

**Three archived copies of the register bracket the row's first public appearance.** The copy of 10 December 2025 does not contain it \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum, as archived on 10 December 2025][ref_mds_addendum_wb_2025_12]\], nor does the copy of 15 January 2026, and the copy of 1 February 2026 does. **The row became public between 31 and 48 days after this article's date**, and 87 to 104 days after the allocation it records. Writing $t\_{\mathrm{a}}$ for the allocation, $t\_{\mathrm{d}}$ for this article's date, $t\_{\mathrm{pub}}$ for the row's first public appearance and $t\_{\mathrm{DARPA}}$ for the announcement,

$$
t_{\mathrm{pub}} - t_{\mathrm{d}} \in [\,31,\ 48\,]\ \text{days}, \qquad t_{\mathrm{pub}} - t_{\mathrm{a}} \in [\,87,\ 104\,]\ \text{days}, \qquad t_{\mathrm{DARPA}} - t_{\mathrm{d}} = 84\ \text{days}.
\tag{3}
$$

The compiler's note on the row, read in the current copy, quotes DARPA's statement that the out-of-sequence number is "a deliberate nod to the revolutionary spirit of 1776" \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\], which is 84 days after this article's date. **This article uses the row as a fact about the aeroplane and dates every use of it.** The [X-69 through X-75][related_post_a366_x69_through_x75_leapfrogged_block] article measured this lag and treats the number's meaning, and neither is revisited here.

## Programme Origin, From the Solicitation to the Critical Design Review

**The programme's history can be told almost entirely from government documents**, which is unusual for a vehicle that has not flown, and the documents disagree with each other and with the contractor in ways worth recording.

### The Solicitation Set the Aeroplane's Envelope Before Any Design Existed

**DARPA's Tactical Technology Office posted solicitation HR001123S0031 on Friday 10 March 2023**, held a proposers' day on 23 March, took abstracts until 31 March and proposals until 5 May, and expected to announce awards in September with work beginning in October \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\]. **The programme was joint from the first slide**, with Headquarters, United States Special Operations Command, and its Special Operations Forces Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Center as partner, and the contracting officer's representative to be that center's deputy programme manager. **The programme manager at the proposers' day was Dr. Andrew Baker** \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\]. The programme page by December 2024 named Ian Higgins \[[DARPA SPRINT programme page, as archived on 24 December 2024][ref_darpa_sprint_wb_2024_12]\], and the announcement of March 2026 gives his rank as commander, United States Navy \[[DARPA on the X-76][ref_darpa_x76]\].

**The solicitation asked for two designs, not one.** Each proposer had to size an Operational System to a representative mission and a Demonstrator X-Plane traceable to it, and only the demonstrator was to be built \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. **The operational mission is specific.** It carries a 5,000 pound payload in a notional cargo bay 30 feet long, 8 feet wide and 7 feet high, hovers out of ground effect at sea level on a 102 degree Fahrenheit day for take-off and at 4,000 feet on a 95 degree day mid-mission and for landing, flies two legs of 350 nautical miles at best-range speed, and dashes at maximum continuous power at 400 knots true airspeed as a threshold and 450 as an objective \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\].

**The demonstrator guidance is the closest thing to a specification of the X-76 that is public.** It reads as follows in the slides.

| Attribute | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Gross take-off weight | 8,000 to 15,000 pounds, "weight range is not limiting" |
| Sustained speed | at least 400 knots true airspeed between 15,000 and 30,000 feet |
| Useful payload | at least 1,000 pounds, mainly for flight test instrumentation |
| Flight test endurance | 1.5 hours |
| Radius | at least 200 nautical miles |
| Load margins | minus 0.5 to plus 2 g |
| Design life | 500 hours, with DARPA's demonstration expected to use 200 or fewer |
| Landing | 12 feet per second sink rate with no damage |

**Three further rules shaped the configuration as much as any number.** The X-plane had to use existing engines, and the government would not supply them. **There was no disk loading, downwash or surface hardness limit**, the proposer being asked instead to explain how the design meets the goal of runway independence. **And the goal was first flight of the demonstrator no more than 42 months from contract award** \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. The solicitation budgeted Phase 1A at the order of 15 million dollars, with 75 million dollars available for Phase 1 in total, and it allowed either a procurement contract or an other transaction. **The answers DARPA posted on 30 March 2023 sharpen four of these rules** \[[SPRINT questions and answers][ref_sprint_qa]\]. The Phase 1 money was 15 million dollars for Phase 1A and 60 million for Phase 1B, "a total split among performers", matching the solicitation's 75 million,

$$
15 + 60 = 75\ \text{million dollars}.
\tag{4}
$$

Engine modifications were allowed, but "modifications that include the engine core are not allowed". A proposer could switch instruments between phases, an other transaction for Phase 1 and a regulation-based contract for Phase 2 being given as the example. **And "the SPRINT X-Plane is not intended to transition to an operational system"** \[[SPRINT questions and answers][ref_sprint_qa]\], which the budget books, describing a demonstrator that transitions for further risk reduction flight testing, do not contradict, since that transition is of the test aircraft and not to production \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\].

### Thirteen Offers and Four Awards, Three of Them in the Contract Record

**The federal award record holds three first-phase contracts and states that each was competed with thirteen offers received.** All three are cost-plus-fixed-fee research contracts under the solicitation's number, described as Speed and Runway Independent Technologies, and the award notices posted to the contracting portal on 2 and 7 November 2023 \[[Award HR001124C0325 to Aurora Flight Sciences][ref_award_aurora]\] \[[Award HR001124C0326 to Piasecki Aircraft][ref_award_piasecki]\] \[[Award HR001124C0327 to Northrop Grumman][ref_award_northrop]\] \[[Award notice for HR001124C0326][ref_sam_notice_0326]\] \[[Award notice for HR001124C0325][ref_sam_notice_0325]\] \[[Award notice for HR001124C0327][ref_sam_notice_0327]\].

| Award | Recipient | Start | Obligated to date |
|---|---|---|---:|
| HR001124C0326 | Piasecki Aircraft | 31 October 2023 | 4,944,700 dollars |
| HR001124C0325 | Aurora Flight Sciences | 1 November 2023 | 33,301,718 dollars |
| HR001124C0327 | Northrop Grumman | 1 November 2023 | 5,406,094 dollars |

**DARPA's programme page dates the programme's entry into Phase 1 to 1 November 2023**, which agrees with two of the three start dates \[[DARPA SPRINT programme page, as archived on 12 December 2025][ref_darpa_sprint_wb_2025_12]\]. Bell announced its selection for Phase 1A on 27 November 2023 \[[Bell selected for SPRINT Phase 1A][ref_bell_phase1a]\]. **The Piasecki and Northrop Grumman contracts' periods of performance end on 30 April 2024** \[[Award HR001124C0326 to Piasecki Aircraft][ref_award_piasecki]\] \[[Award HR001124C0327 to Northrop Grumman][ref_award_northrop]\], the point at which the record shows their participation stopping.

### Bell's Instrument Is Not in the Contract Record

**No contract, grant or indefinite-delivery vehicle from DARPA to any Bell entity for this programme appears in the award record**, searched by programme name, by the phrases speed and runway and runway independent, and by recipient. **The solicitation allowed an other transaction, and its answers allowed a different instrument in each phase** \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\] \[[SPRINT questions and answers][ref_sprint_qa]\]. An other transaction is not a procurement contract, and no document read here states whether or how DARPA reports one to the award record, so the absence is consistent with Bell holding one. **The point is inferred.** Bell's instrument, its value and its date are named in none of them, and the article's statements about money are confined to what the record holds.

### Phase 1B, and the Money the Record Allows Bell

**Aurora's contract carries both phases, and its modifications date the Phase 1B decision.** The obligations before 24 May 2024 total 4,843,311 dollars, and modification P00006 on 24 May 2024 obligates 12,974,331 dollars, after which a further 15,484,076 dollars follow through February 2025 \[[Award HR001124C0325 to Aurora Flight Sciences][ref_award_aurora]\]. **That date agrees with DARPA's statement that Aurora and Bell were awarded Phase 1B in May 2024** \[[DARPA SPRINT programme page, as archived on 12 December 2025][ref_darpa_sprint_wb_2025_12]\] and with Bell's release of 28 May 2024 \[[Bell awarded funding for SPRINT Phase 1B][ref_bell_phase1b]\]. The contract's total decomposes exactly into the three periods,

$$
4{,}843{,}311 + 12{,}974{,}331 + 15{,}484{,}076 = 33{,}301{,}718\ \text{dollars}.
\tag{5}
$$

**The three recorded Phase 1A obligations sum to 15,194,105 dollars**, Aurora's pre-option figure with Piasecki's and Northrop Grumman's totals,

$$
4{,}843{,}311 + 4{,}944{,}700 + 5{,}406{,}094 = 15{,}194{,}105 = 15{,}000{,}000 + 194{,}105\ \text{dollars},
\tag{6}
$$

**which already exceeds the solicitation's Phase 1A figure by 194,105 dollars before Bell's share is counted.** So the planning figure for Phase 1A was not a cap on what was obligated, and a figure that was not a cap for one sub-phase is weak evidence of a cap for the phase. **The three recorded contracts together total 43,652,512 dollars**, and if the solicitation's 75 million dollars for Phase 1 had held as a ceiling,

$$
B_{\mathrm{Bell}} \le 75{,}000{,}000 - (33{,}301{,}718 + 4{,}944{,}700 + 5{,}406{,}094) = 31{,}347{,}488\ \text{dollars}.
\tag{7}
$$

**Bell's Phase 1 instrument could then not have exceeded 31,347,488 dollars, but the Phase 1A overrun shows that the premise of that bound did not hold for the first sub-phase**, so it is stated as the bound the planning figure implies and not as an estimate of what Bell received.

**Aurora's contract has one more feature that this article records without interpreting.** Its last modification, on 27 August 2025, carries the description `DARPA RESEARCH PROJECT` in place of the programme's name, and its period of performance ends on 21 October 2025, the day after the X-76A allocation \[[Award HR001124C0325 to Aurora Flight Sciences][ref_award_aurora]\].

### The Other Finalist Also Chose Two Kinds of Engine

**Aurora's releases describe the design Bell beat, and it shares the X-76's propulsion answer while differing in everything else.** Aurora's release of 20 May 2024 describes a "low-drag, fan-in-wing demonstrator that integrates a blended wing body platform" with three lift fans and "an uncrewed cockpit", capable of 450 knots and using "existing engine solutions" \[[Aurora on its SPRINT design, May 2024][ref_aurora_may24]\]. **Its release of 8 October 2024 is more specific.** The demonstrator was uncrewed, with a 45-foot wingspan and a 1,000 pound payload, and "the propulsion system includes off-the-shelf turbofan and turboshaft engines that would power the vehicle to a maximum of 450 knots true airspeed" \[[Aurora on its SPRINT design, October 2024][ref_aurora_oct24]\].

**Both Phase 1B designs carried a turbofan and a turboshaft** \[[Aurora on its SPRINT design, October 2024][ref_aurora_oct24]\] \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. One buried its lift fans in a blended wing and the other folded its rotors, and both answered the solicitation's existing-engine rule with two kinds of engine rather than one convertible machine. **It is the strongest evidence in the record that the separate-engine choice came from the rule rather than from Bell**, evidence drawn from the competitor's documents. The October 2024 release also gives the schedule as it then stood, with preliminary design review "scheduled for April 2025", the phase running "through May 2025", and "flight testing for the program is planned for 2027" \[[Aurora on its SPRINT design, October 2024][ref_aurora_oct24]\].

### Phase 2 Began in May, June or July 2025, Depending on Who Is Asked

**Three sources inside or near the date give three months for the same decision.** DARPA's programme page reports that in June 2025 Bell "was awarded a contract for Phases 2 and 3" \[[DARPA SPRINT programme page, as archived on 12 December 2025][ref_darpa_sprint_wb_2025_12]\]. Bell announced its selection for Phase 2 on 9 July 2025 \[[Bell to build the SPRINT X-plane][ref_bell_phase2]\]. **DARPA's announcement of March 2026 states that the programme began its second phase in May 2025 "following the downselect to Bell"** \[[DARPA on the X-76][ref_darpa_x76]\]. These can all be true at once, a selection in May, an award in June and an announcement in July, but **no document read here identifies which event each date names**, and the article does not choose.

**The contractor's account of what Phase 2 includes changed between its releases.** The release of July 2025 describes Phase 2 as "design, construction, ground testing and certification of an X-plane demonstrator" \[[Bell to build the SPRINT X-plane][ref_bell_phase2]\], while the solicitation had placed Phase 2 as critical design, build and ground test and Phase 3 as flight test \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. **The certification in that sentence is airworthiness certification for an experimental aircraft**, which the solicitation also placed in Phase 2, following a DARPA flight release tailored from the airworthiness handbook MIL-HDBK-516C \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\].

### Two Contractor Datelines Are a Year Early on One Mirror

**Textron's investor-relations copies of two Bell releases carry datelines a year earlier than the releases themselves.** The Phase 1B release, listed under 2024 and describing events of late 2023, is datelined "May 28, 2023" in its body \[[Textron copy of the Phase 1B release][ref_textron_phase1b]\]. The Phase 2 release, listed under 2025, is datelined "July 9, 2024" \[[Textron copy of the Phase 2 release][ref_textron_phase2]\]. **Bell's own newsroom carries the correct dates**, 28 May 2024 for the first and 9 July 2025 for the second \[[Bell awarded funding for SPRINT Phase 1B][ref_bell_phase1b]\] \[[Bell to build the SPRINT X-plane][ref_bell_phase2]\], so the error lies in the mirror and not in the contractor's record. **It is recorded because a reader who took either dateline from the mirror would place Phase 1B before Phase 1A existed**, and a chronology built from mirrored releases would be wrong by exactly a year in two places.

### The Schedule Has Moved by at Least Eight Months

**The solicitation's goal of first flight within 42 months of contract award puts first flight by 1 May 2027 for an award on 1 November 2023.** The slides' notional schedule draws first flight in fiscal year 2027 for each notional performer \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\]. **As late as October 2024 the programme planned flight testing for 2027**, by Aurora's account of the schedule it was working to \[[Aurora on its SPRINT design, October 2024][ref_aurora_oct24]\]. **By July 2025 it planned flight testing in 2028**, so the slip arose between those two dates, across the preliminary design review. Inside this article's date, a DARPA spokesperson told Breaking Defense in July 2025 that the agency expected a completed demonstrator in 2027 and flight testing in 2028 \[[Breaking Defense on the Phase 2 selection][ref_bd_phase2]\], and DARPA's March 2026 announcement, after it, gives early 2028 \[[DARPA on the X-76][ref_darpa_x76]\]. **Taking early 2028 as 1 January 2028, the slip is at least eight months, and first flight would come at least 50 months after the Phase 1 award.** Counting calendar months from the award,

$$
t_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\mathrm{goal}} = t_{\mathrm{award}} + 42\ \text{months} = 1\ \text{May}\ 2027, \qquad t_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\mathrm{plan}} - t_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\mathrm{goal}} \ge 8\ \text{months}, \qquad t_{\mathrm{ff}}^{\mathrm{plan}} - t_{\mathrm{award}} \ge 50\ \text{months},
\tag{8}
$$

and the 42-month goal is 1,277 days. **The programme's other intervals set the pace against which that slip is measured**, 236 days from the solicitation's posting to the first award, and 719 days from that award to the designation's allocation,

$$
t_{\mathrm{award}} - t_{\mathrm{BAA}} = 236\ \text{days}, \qquad t_{\mathrm{a}} - t_{\mathrm{award}} = 719\ \text{days}.
\tag{9}
$$

The comparison is between a goal and a plan, both of them documents, and implies no engineering difficulty, since no source read for this article describes one.

## What Four Budget Books Said

**DARPA's research, development, test and evaluation budget justification books carry a programme entry for this programme in fiscal years 2024 through 2027**, three of them published before 15 December 2025 and the fourth, of April 2026, after it \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2024][ref_darpa_pb2024]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2025][ref_darpa_pb2025]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2027][ref_darpa_pb2027]\]. The entry sits in programme element 0603286E, Advanced Aerospace Systems, until fiscal year 2026, when it moves to programme element 0603468E, Advanced Complex Systems, project ACX-01, along with other programmes of the same project, among them the X-planes of the [X-65][related_post_a362_aurora_x65_crane] and [X-68][related_post_a365_general_atomics_x68_longshot] articles.

### The Same Year Reported Three Ways

**Each book restates the earlier years, and the restatements are large.** Figures are millions of dollars.

| Book for fiscal year, and its date | 2024 | 2025 | 2026 | 2027 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 2024, March 2023 | 22.663 | | | |
| 2025, March 2024 | 22.663 | 36.866 | | |
| 2026, June 2025 | 13.024 | 41.998 | 55.200 | |
| 2027, April 2026, outside the date | | 47.000 | 47.524 | 62.113 |

**Fiscal year 2024 was requested at 22.663 million and executed at 13.024 million**, a shortfall of 9.639 million in the programme's first year \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2024][ref_darpa_pb2024]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\]. **Fiscal year 2025 grew from a request of 36.866 million to an actual of 47.000 million in the latest book**, about 27.5 percent more \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2025][ref_darpa_pb2025]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2027][ref_darpa_pb2027]\]. **Fiscal year 2026 was requested at 55.200 million and the latest book carries 47.524 million**, about 13.9 percent less, though that figure is the current-year column of the latest book rather than an execution \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2027][ref_darpa_pb2027]\]. **The latest figures for fiscal years 2024 through 2027 sum to 169.661 million dollars.** In millions,

$$
22.663 - 13.024 = 9.639, \qquad \frac{47.000}{36.866} - 1 = 0.275, \qquad 1 - \frac{47.524}{55.200} = 0.139, \qquad 13.024 + 47.000 + 47.524 + 62.113 = 169.661.
\tag{10}
$$

None of these figures is a contract value, and none of them can be reconciled with the award record's 43.65 million without Bell's missing instrument.

### A Scaled Demonstrator Became a Demonstrator

**The fiscal year 2024 book describes a programme that "culminates in the fabrication and flight test of a scaled demonstrator."** \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2024][ref_darpa_pb2024]\] The fiscal year 2025 book, a year later, drops the word scaled, and every later book follows it \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2025][ref_darpa_pb2025]\]. The solicitation itself had asked for "a scaled X-Plane demonstrator to validate the enabling technologies at a relevant size" \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. **This article reads the change as vocabulary rather than concept**, since the demonstrator guidance of 8,000 to 15,000 pounds was already a scale relative to the operational system and nothing in the plans changes, but it records the change because the word scaled is the only statement in any budget book about the aircraft's size relative to anything.

### The Transition Partner Changed Its Name Four Times

**Each book names who the demonstrator transitions to, and each names it differently.** The fiscal year 2024 book reads "military service members", the 2025 book "military services", the 2026 book "a DoD component" and the 2027 book "a Services component" \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2024][ref_darpa_pb2024]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2025][ref_darpa_pb2025]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\] \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2027][ref_darpa_pb2027]\]. **The 2027 book also rewrites the missions**, adding contested logistics under attack and electronic warfare and dropping logistics support and the sentence that "the thresholds for speed and range have evolved with military strategy and mission needs" \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2027][ref_darpa_pb2027]\]. **Special Operations Command is not named anywhere in the programme's entries in any book**, its only appearance being the books' tables of contents, although it is named as the joint partner on every DARPA page and in the solicitation.

### The Plans Describe an Aircraft Flown From a Ground Station

**The plans lists are the closest thing to a schedule the books hold, and they read in sequence.** The 2024 book plans conceptual design review "for multiple concepts" \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2024][ref_darpa_pb2024]\]. The 2025 book plans preliminary design review and the start of limited detailed and critical design \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2025][ref_darpa_pb2025]\]. **The 2026 book, dated June 2025 and inside the date, plans the subsystems by name**, "propulsion system, thermal management system, hydraulics, electrical system", along with control law development, engineering drawing release, airworthiness certification, integration with the flight test facility, manufacture of the demonstrator, and "ground station and human-machine interface development" \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\]. **The 2027 book, outside the date, adds a structural proof load test, final software integration laboratory testing with simulated failures, and ground checkouts "including engine runs"** \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2027][ref_darpa_pb2027]\].

**A thermal management system appears by name in the subsystem list.** This article cannot say why, and records only that an aircraft carrying at least three gas turbines, two of which may idle or shut down in cruise, has more than one heat source to manage.

## Sizing From First Principles

**Nothing about the X-76's mass, wing, rotor diameter or drag is public at this article's date, nor in any later document read for it.** What is public is the solicitation's envelope and the certificated ratings of the engines the register names, taken as two turboshafts and one turbofan. **This section does not estimate the aeroplane.** It derives what those engines can do for any aeroplane inside the envelope, which bounds the X-76 from both ends.

**Every input is one of three kinds and the text names which.** Engine ratings and masses are certificated figures from the type-certificate data sheets. The weight range, speed band and altitude band are the solicitation's. **Everything else is a named assumption, swept where a result depends on it**, and the assumptions are the hover figure of merit, the transmission efficiency, the wing download, the thrust lapse factor, the helical tip Mach limit and the maximum lift coefficient. Results that depend on an assumption say so where they are stated.

### The Symbols This Article Uses

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |

| $W$ | gross weight | N |
| $m\_0$ | gross mass, with $W = m\_0 g$ | kg |
| $g$ | standard gravitational acceleration, 9.80665 | m/s² |

| $\mu\_e$ | engine mass fraction, $m\_e / m\_0$ | none |
