| $B\_{\mathrm{Bell}}$ | the value of Bell's Phase 1 instrument | dollars |

### The Atmosphere

**Every density and speed of sound below comes from the standard troposphere**, the 1976 standard's constants applied with the hydrostatic relation \[[U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 1976][ref_atm76]\]. Below 11 kilometres,

$$
T = T_0 - \Lambda h, \qquad p = p_0 \left( \frac{T}{T_0} \right)^{g / (\Lambda R)}, \qquad \rho = \frac{p}{R T}, \qquad a = \sqrt{\gamma R T}.
\tag{11}
$$

**The solicitation's hover condition is 4,000 feet on a 95 degree Fahrenheit day** \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\], which the slides give as an altitude and a temperature without naming the kind of altitude, and which this article reads as a pressure altitude. Holding pressure on the standard profile and raising temperature to 308.15 kelvin gives a density of 0.9893 kilograms per cubic metre, a density ratio of 0.8076. **Since induced power at fixed weight and disk area scales as the inverse square root of density**, the hot-day condition costs

$$
\sqrt{\frac{\rho_0}{\rho_{\mathrm{hot}}}} = \sqrt{\frac{1.225}{0.9893}} = 1.113,
\tag{12}
$$

an 11.3 percent increase in induced power, before any loss of engine power with temperature, which this article does not model. **The turboshafts' hot-day lapse appears in none of the sources**, so every hot-day result below is optimistic by that unmodelled amount.

### The Installed Power and What It Hovers

**The certificated CT7-8 delivers 1,879 kilowatts, 2,520 shaft horsepower, at its five-minute take-off rating and 1,523 kilowatts at maximum continuous, with a dry mass of 243.6 kilograms** \[[Type-certificate data sheet for the CT7 series][ref_easa_ct7]\]. The register names the model as `CT7-8` without a suffix \[[Parsch, DOD 4120.15-L Addendum][ref_mds_addendum]\]. **The same data sheet lists the suffixed CT7-8 models from 1,845 to 2,009 kilowatts at take-off**, so if the register's name stands for the family rather than the base model, the installed power lies between about 2 percent below and 7 percent above the base figure,

$$
\frac{1845}{1879} = 0.982, \qquad \frac{2009}{1879} = 1.069.
\tag{13}
$$

Two engines give

$$
P = 2 \times 1879\ \text{kW} = 3758\ \text{kW}
\tag{14}
$$

at take-off and 3,046 kilowatts at maximum continuous.

**Momentum theory gives the power to hover in terms of disk loading alone.** An ideal rotor producing thrust $W(1+d)$ through a disk of area $A$ needs an induced power equal to that thrust times the induced velocity, and a real one needs that power divided by its figure of merit and by the drive system's efficiency. With $w = W / A$,

$$
P_h = \frac{W (1 + d)^{3/2}}{\mathrm{FM}\, \eta} \sqrt{\frac{w}{2 \rho}}.
\tag{15}
$$

**Setting $P\_h$ equal to the installed power and solving for weight gives the heaviest aeroplane the two turboshafts can hover at a chosen disk loading**,

$$
W_{\max} = \frac{P\, \mathrm{FM}\, \eta}{(1 + d)^{3/2}} \sqrt{\frac{2 \rho}{w}},
\tag{16}
$$

and solving instead for disk loading at the solicitation's heaviest weight gives the highest disk loading at which that weight can still hover,

$$
w_{\max} = 2 \rho \left( \frac{P\, \mathrm{FM}\, \eta}{W (1 + d)^{3/2}} \right)^{2}.
\tag{17}
$$

**These depend on the three hover assumptions, and the table states them at the assumed values.** None of the three is taken from a measurement of the X-76 or quoted from a report. The figure of merit of full-scale tiltrotor proprotors was measured at Ames Research Center's outdoor facility in the 1980s, for the XV-15's metal and composite blades and a model of the V-22's \[[Felker et al. 1986a][research_felker_maisel_1986]\] \[[Felker et al. 1985][research_felker_betzina_1985]\], and the magnitude of the wing download for typical tiltrotor configurations is the subject of a review of that research \[[Felker 1988][research_felker_1988]\]. **This article read those reports' abstracts and one report's text, and it does not quote a figure from them**, because the measured values sit in plotted and tabulated data whose extracted text is not reliable. The assumed values are typical of that literature's subject and are labelled as assumptions throughout. Weights are in pounds, disk loadings in pounds per square foot, and the power fraction is the share of the two engines' take-off power needed to hover 15,000 pounds at sea level.

| Disk loading | Heaviest hover weight, sea level | Heaviest hover weight, 4,000 ft and 95 °F | Power fraction at 15,000 lb | Radius of each rotor at 15,000 lb |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 10 | 35,358 | 31,775 | 0.424 | 4.71 m |
| 13.2, the XV-15's | 30,775 | 27,657 | 0.487 | 4.10 m |
| 15 | 28,870 | 25,944 | 0.520 | 3.85 m |
| 20 | 25,002 | 22,469 | 0.600 | 3.33 m |
| 30 | 20,414 | 18,345 | 0.735 | 2.72 m |
| 60 | 14,435 | 12,972 | 1.039 | 1.92 m |

**The XV-15's disk loading of 13.2 pounds per square foot is its published figure, at a design gross weight of 13,000 pounds on two 25-foot proprotors** \[[The History of the XV-15 Tilt Rotor Research Aircraft][ref_xv15_history]\]. Each rotor's radius follows from the total disk area shared by two equal rotors,

$$
r = \sqrt{\frac{W}{2 \pi w}}.
\tag{18}
$$

**Two CT7-8s hover 15,000 pounds at sea level at any disk loading up to about 55.6 pounds per square foot**, which corresponds to rotors of about 4.0 metres diameter each. Since the limit is proportional to density, on the solicitation's hot day before engine lapse it falls to

$$
w_{\max}^{\mathrm{hot}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{hot}}\, w_{\max} = 0.8076 \times 55.6\ \text{psf} = 44.9\ \text{psf}.
\tag{19}
$$

**At the XV-15's disk loading they would hover about 30,800 pounds at sea level**, twice the solicitation's heaviest figure,

$$
\frac{W_{\max}(w = 13.2\ \text{psf})}{15{,}000\ \text{lb}} = \frac{30{,}775}{15{,}000} = 2.05.
\tag{20}
$$

**Every hot-day weight in the table is the same fraction of its sea-level neighbour**, because the heaviest hover weight scales as the square root of density at fixed power and disk loading,

$$
\frac{W_{\max}(\rho_{\mathrm{hot}})}{W_{\max}(\rho_0)} = \sqrt{\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{hot}}}{\rho_0}} = \sqrt{0.8076} = 0.899,
\tag{21}
$$

the hot day's 10 percent penalty on hover weight before any engine lapse. **The turboshafts are not the constraint on the X-76's weight at any conventional tiltrotor disk loading.** Either the aircraft is heavier than the solicitation's guidance, which the guidance explicitly permits, or it hovers with a large power margin, or it hovers at a disk loading well above a conventional tiltrotor's, and the engines alone cannot say which. **Two observations favour the third.** Folded blades must lie along their nacelles, and Bell's patent on a stowed-blade clamp describes a blade "foldable to a stowed position extending substantially parallel to the pylon" \[[US 2021/0078695][ref_pat_us20210078695]\], so blade length is bounded by nacelle length. And the solicitation set no disk loading limit \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. **Both are inferences about the X-76, not facts about it.**

### Disk Loading Is the Price of Runway Independence

**The solicitation asks for hover over unprepared surfaces with personnel nearby and then declines to limit disk loading, downwash or surface hardness**, asking the proposer to explain how the design meets the goal instead \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. **Momentum theory makes the trade explicit.** The induced velocity at the disk is

$$
v_h = \sqrt{\frac{(1 + d)\, w}{2 \rho}},
\tag{22}
$$

and the fully developed wake below an ideal rotor moves at twice that. At sea level, the XV-15's disk loading gives 16.8 metres per second at the disk and 33.7 in the wake. **A disk loading of 20 gives 20.7 and 41.5, and a disk loading of 60 gives 35.9 and 71.8.** The wake speed rises with the square root of disk loading. **What the ground and a person standing on it feel is the wake's dynamic pressure, and that has a cleaner form**, since squaring twice the induced velocity cancels the density,

$$
q_w = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho \left( 2 v_h \right)^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} \rho \cdot \frac{4 (1 + d)\, w}{2 \rho} = (1 + d)\, w.
\tag{23}
$$

**The fully developed wake's dynamic pressure equals the rotor's thrust per unit disk area, at any altitude and on any day.** At the XV-15's disk loading it is 695 pascals, 14.5 pounds per square foot, at a disk loading of 20 it is 1,053 pascals, and at 60 it is 3,160 pascals, 66 pounds per square foot. **A stop-fold aircraft that shortens its blades to stow them pays for cruise speed in downwash, in exact proportion to the disk loading it accepts**, and downwash is the quantity runway independence is about. The literature on outwash and its effect on people standing near a hovering aircraft is cited in the survey below, and one of its studies is titled for that question \[[Calvert and Wenren 2019][research_calvert_wenren_2019_2]\], which this article cites for its title only.

### The Jet Is a Drag Budget

**The certificated PW308C produces 31.15 kilonewtons at its five-minute take-off rating and 31.13 kilonewtons at maximum continuous, at sea-level static conditions, with a dry mass of 623.5 kilograms** \[[Type-certificate data sheet for the PW308 series][ref_easa_pw308]\]. **How that thrust falls with altitude and speed is not in the data sheet or in any other source this article found.** This article therefore models it in the simplest form consistent with turbofan behaviour, thrust falling with density at a fixed Mach factor,

$$
F = F_0\, \sigma\, \varphi,
\tag{24}
$$

and sweeps the factor $\varphi$ from 0.5 to 0.7 at cruise Mach numbers. **That range is an assumption, not a measurement of this engine**, and the results are stated across it.

**In steady level flight thrust equals drag.** Writing the aircraft's total drag as the dynamic pressure times an equivalent flat-plate area, $D = q f$, and noting that the thrust available is an upper bound on the drag that can be carried,

$$
f_{\max} = \frac{F}{q} = \frac{F_0\, \sigma\, \varphi}{\tfrac{1}{2} \sigma \rho_0 V^2} = \frac{2 F_0\, \varphi}{\rho_0 V^2}.
\tag{25}
$$

**The density ratio cancels, so the largest drag area the jet can push at a given true airspeed is the same at every altitude**, to the extent that the lapse factor is. At 400 knots true airspeed the coefficient $2 F\_0 / (\rho\_0 V^2)$ is 1.200 square metres and at 450 knots it is 0.948. **Across the swept lapse factor, the X-76 can carry at most 0.60 to 0.84 square metres of equivalent drag area at 400 knots, 6.5 to 9.0 square feet, and 0.47 to 0.66 square metres at 450 knots.** That budget includes the induced drag of lifting the aircraft, so the parasite budget is smaller still. **It must hold the fuselage, the wing, two nacelles with their folded blades, the tails and the inlet**, which explains why the folded configuration has to be clean and why Bell has patented a chined spinner and blade fairings for the folded rotor, the abstract describing blades "folded down" in forward flight against fairings that cover them \[[US 12,030,623][ref_pat_us12030623]\].

**The same model gives the lift-to-drag ratio the aircraft must reach.** Thrust equal to drag and lift equal to weight require

$$
\left( \frac{L}{D} \right)_{\mathrm{req}} = \frac{W}{F} = \frac{W}{F_0\, \sigma\, \varphi}.
\tag{26}
$$

At 15,000 pounds and the middle of the lapse range, the required ratio is 5.68 at 15,000 feet, 6.70 at 20,000, 7.97 at 25,000 and 9.55 at 30,000. At 8,000 pounds it is 3.03 at 15,000 feet and 5.09 at 30,000. **The requirement rises with altitude because thrust falls with density while weight does not**, so the bottom of the solicitation's altitude band is where the turbofan most easily meets the speed requirement, and **a heavy X-76 would most plausibly demonstrate 400 knots near 15,000 feet.** The claim follows from the model alone. **Turned around, the same relation gives the highest altitude at which a given lift-to-drag ratio still allows 400 knots**, since level flight needs the density ratio to be at least

$$
\sigma_{\min} = \frac{W}{F_0\, \varphi\, E},
\tag{27}
$$

which at 15,000 pounds and the middle of the lapse range is 0.595 for $E = 6$, 0.447 for $E = 8$ and 0.357 for $E = 10$, standard-atmosphere altitudes of about 16,700, 25,100 and 31,200 feet. **A lift-to-drag ratio near 6 in the folded cruise configuration would confine a 15,000 pound X-76 to the bottom of the solicitation's band**, and the band's top needs a ratio near 10.

**The turbofan's thrust power is comparable to the turboshafts' shaft power.** At 400 knots and 15,000 feet, at the middle of the lapse range,

$$
P_F = F V = 31.13\ \text{kN} \times 0.6292 \times 0.6 \times 205.8\ \text{m/s} = 2.42\ \text{MW},
\tag{28}
$$

against 3.05 megawatts of maximum continuous shaft power from the two CT7-8s,

$$
\frac{P_F}{P_{\mathrm{mcp}}} = \frac{2.42\ \text{MW}}{3.05\ \text{MW}} = 0.79.
\tag{29}
$$

**The aircraft thus carries two power sources of the same order and uses one at a time**, the cost of having two propulsion systems and the reason Bell's patents describe drive systems that let an otherwise idle lift engine contribute thrust in cruise through a pylon-mounted ducted fan \[[US 11,325,719][ref_pat_us11325719]\], or that couple and decouple rotors and thrust fans through clutches in one gearbox \[[US 11,577,831][ref_pat_us11577831]\]. **Whether the X-76 does either has not been disclosed.**

### The Proprotor's Speed Limit Forces the Rotor to Stop

**A proprotor in axial flight sees its blade tip moving at its own tip speed and the aircraft's speed at right angles**, so the helical tip Mach number, the variable against which the advanced high-speed propeller programme measured its noise \[[Dittmar and Hall 1991][research_dittmar_hall_1991]\], is

$$
M_h = \frac{\sqrt{V^2 + V_t^2}}{a}.
\tag{30}
$$

**The XV-15 turned its 25-foot proprotors at 517 revolutions per minute in airplane mode and 589 in helicopter mode**, tip speeds of 206.3 and 235.0 metres per second \[[The History of the XV-15 Tilt Rotor Research Aircraft][ref_xv15_history]\]. **The hover figure can be checked against a measurement.** At sea level 235.0 metres per second is a tip Mach number of 0.69, inside the range of 0.60 to 0.73 over which a full-scale XV-15 rotor's hover performance was measured, a range across which that test found "very little effect on rotor performance due to tip Mach number variations" \[[Felker et al. 1985][research_felker_betzina_1985]\]. The height-velocity envelope in that history's appendix reaches about 300 knots true at 16,000 feet \[[The History of the XV-15 Tilt Rotor Research Aircraft][ref_xv15_history]\], where its airplane-mode helical tip Mach number is 0.80. **At the X-76's speeds the same tip speed is no longer workable.** At 400 knots and 15,000 feet it gives 0.90, and at 450 knots and 25,000 feet it gives 1.00, a tip that is sonic.

**Holding the helical tip Mach number to a limit fixes the largest tip speed a proprotor may turn at**,

$$
V_t \le a \sqrt{M_{h,\max}^2 - M^2},
\tag{31}
$$

and taking 0.85 as that limit, which is an assumption, the XV-15's airplane-mode tip speed is exceeded above 350 knots at 15,000 feet and above 318 knots at 25,000. **To hold the limit at 450 knots and 25,000 feet the rotor would have to turn at about 61 percent of that tip speed**, and at 400 knots and 15,000 feet at about 88 percent. **And at an airspeed equal to the limit times the speed of sound no tip speed at all satisfies it**,

$$
V_{\mathrm{wall}} = M_{h,\max}\, a,
\tag{32}
$$

which is 532 knots at 15,000 feet and 512 knots at 25,000. **The objective of 450 knots is therefore not beyond the compressibility wall**, but it is in the region where a proprotor must be slowed so far that its advance ratio is high and its thrust per unit of tip speed is poor. **The two quantities make that concrete.** The tip speed allowed as a fraction of the XV-15's, and the advance ratio that results, are

$$
\kappa = \frac{a \sqrt{M_{h,\max}^2 - M^2}}{V_t^{\mathrm{XV15}}}, \qquad \lambda = \frac{V}{\kappa\, V_t^{\mathrm{XV15}}},
\tag{33}
$$

which give $\kappa = 0.877$ and $\lambda = 1.14$ at 400 knots and 15,000 feet, and $\kappa = 0.607$ and $\lambda = 1.85$ at 450 knots and 25,000 feet. **The XV-15 at its 300 knots ran at an advance ratio of 0.75**, so the X-76's objective asks a proprotor for two and a half times the advance ratio of the aircraft that proved the configuration. That, with whirl flutter, is the case for stopping the rotor rather than slowing it. **Bell's paper states the conclusion and not this arithmetic**, that the stop-fold configuration can "make the rotor disappear" in cruise \[[Schank et al. 2025][research_schank_xin_2025]\].

### The Conversion Must Happen Where the Wing Can Fly

**The rotor can only be stopped once the wing is carrying the whole weight and the jet the whole drag.** The lower bound on the speed at which that is possible is the wing's stall speed,

$$
V_s = \sqrt{\frac{2\, (W/S)}{\rho_0\, C_{L}^{\max}}},
\tag{34}
$$

which at sea level, taking a maximum lift coefficient of 1.6, is 105 knots at a wing loading of 60 pounds per square foot, 122 at 80 and 136 at 100. **The wing loading of the X-76 is not public and those three values are illustrative.** The historical literature puts the stopping speed in the range that result implies. Engle and Sambell placed rotor stopping "in the 120 to 200-knot speed range" in 1969 \[[Engle and Sambell 1969][research_engle_sambell_1969]\], and the full-scale folding rotor tested in 1972 completed more than forty start and stop sequences at tunnel speeds up to 175 knots, making "smooth start/stop transitions" in about two seconds \[[Large Scale Wind Tunnel 1972][research_reportcr114464_1972]\]. **The conversion corridor of a stop-fold aircraft is therefore a band bounded below by the wing, at the illustrative stall speeds between 105 and 136 knots, and above by the loads on a rotor being stopped and on blades being folded in a moving airstream, which the historical tests put between 175 and 200 knots**, and a stopped blade at the wrong angle can go unstable in a way a turning blade does not, a full-scale test having found "violent dynamic instabilities" of a stopped blade that its author concluded were a type of stall flutter \[[White 1969][research_white_1969]\].

### The Engines Alone Are a Sixth of the Heaviest Aeroplane

**On the one-turbofan reading, the three engines' dry masses sum to 1,110.7 kilograms, 2,449 pounds**, 487.2 kilograms of turboshaft and 623.5 of turbofan,

$$
m_e = 2 \times 243.6 + 623.5 = 1110.7\ \text{kg}.
\tag{35}
$$

As a fraction of gross mass,

$$
\mu_e = \frac{m_e}{m_0} = \frac{1110.7\ \text{kg}}{6803.9\ \text{kg}} = 0.163 \quad \text{at 15,000 lb}, \qquad \frac{1110.7\ \text{kg}}{3628.7\ \text{kg}} = 0.306 \quad \text{at 8,000 lb}.
\tag{36}
$$

**Bare engines at 16 percent of gross mass, before transmissions, shafts, the fold mechanism, inlets and nacelles, put the X-76 at the heavy end of the solicitation's range or above it.** At the light end the bare engines alone would be almost a third of the aircraft. **This is the article's one line of evidence that the demonstrator is heavier than 15,000 pounds or close to it**, an inference from certificated engine data and not a statement about the aircraft. The hover power margin is not a second line, because the section on installed power found that it is equally consistent with a heavier aircraft, a large power margin or a high disk loading, and that two observations favour the high disk loading. The turboshafts' specific power and the turbofan's static thrust-to-weight ratio are

$$
\frac{1879\ \text{kW}}{243.6\ \text{kg}} = 7.7\ \text{kW/kg}, \qquad \frac{31.15\ \text{kN}}{623.5\ \text{kg} \times g} = 5.1,
\tag{37}
$$

so **the turbofan is the heavier of the two systems for the job it does**, carrying the aircraft only in the one flight phase that a proprotor cannot reach. **And the turbofan alone could not lift the aircraft.** Its static thrust is a fraction of the weight at both ends of the solicitation's range,

$$
\frac{F_0}{W} = \frac{31.15\ \text{kN}}{66.72\ \text{kN}} = 0.47 \quad \text{at 15,000 lb}, \qquad \frac{31.15\ \text{kN}}{35.59\ \text{kN}} = 0.88 \quad \text{at 8,000 lb},
\tag{38}
$$

so even a jet vectored downward could not hover the X-76. The hover must be the rotors', and the conversion is a hand-over between two systems rather than a change of attitude of one.

## The Concept Is Older Than the Programme

**Bell's July 2025 release calls the aircraft that became the X-76 "a brand-new aircraft with the first-ever stop/fold technology"** \[[Bell to build the SPRINT X-plane][ref_bell_phase2]\]. **The aircraft is new, and the idea is at least sixty years older in the open literature**, where a 1964 paper considered stopping a rotor in forward flight \[[Celniker et al. 1964][research_celniker_culver_1964]\] and a 1965 paper described a stowed-rotor concept for vertical and short take-off and landing \[[Leoni and Kaplita 1965][research_leoni_kaplita_1965]\], and the programme's design choices make most sense read against what that literature found.

### Bell Stopped and Folded a Full-Scale Rotor in 1972

**The configuration was studied as a family of aircraft from the late 1960s.** Engle and Sambell's 1969 paper on folding-proprotor performance describes "moderate disc loading for efficient vertical lift and cruise speeds of 400 knots and beyond" \[[Engle and Sambell 1969][research_engle_sambell_1969]\]. DeTore and Gaffey's paper on the stopped-rotor variant of the proprotor aircraft was presented in 1969 and published in 1970 \[[Detore and Gaffey 1969][research_detore_gaffey_1969]\] \[[DeTore and Gaffey 1970][research_detore_gaffey_1970]\], and a paper on the stability and control of a tilt-fold-proprotor aircraft followed the same path in 1970 and 1971 \[[Nicholson and Tiller 1970][research_nicholson_tiller_1970]\] \[[Tiller and Nicholson 1971][research_tiller_nicholson_1971]\], all cited here for their titles only. **A wind tunnel test of the conversion process of a folding tilt rotor, using an unpowered semispan model, is also from 1971** \[[Magee and Taylor 1971][research_magee_taylor_1971]\], again cited for its title.

**In February 1972 a folding version of Bell's 25-foot proprotor was tested in the 40 by 80 foot wind tunnel at Ames Research Center**, in a programme jointly funded by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, the Army and the Air Force with Bell as hardware contractor. The XV-15's official history records that the stop-fold tilt rotor "eliminated the rotor/pylon/wing aeroelastic instability by stopping the rotor while in the airplane configuration", that the blades were folded back along the nacelle to cut their drag, and that "a convertible engine was used to produce the jet thrust" \[[The History of the XV-15 Tilt Rotor Research Aircraft][ref_xv15_history]\]. **The test report records more than forty start and stop sequences, with smooth transitions in about two seconds at tunnel speeds up to 175 knots** \[[Large Scale Wind Tunnel 1972][research_reportcr114464_1972]\].

**And the history records why the idea was then shelved.** The stop-fold tilt rotor "had the additional penalties of the increased complexity and increased weight of the stop/fold mechanism, and, with the lack of a developed convertible engine, it was put aside as a potentially feasible concept that would require further advancements to be an effective contender" \[[The History of the XV-15 Tilt Rotor Research Aircraft][ref_xv15_history]\]. **Two of the three obstacles named in that sentence are obstacles the X-76 accepts, weight and complexity, and the third is one it goes around.**

### The Convertible Engine Was the Missing Piece and the X-76 Does Without It

**For two decades after 1972 the folding tiltrotor's literature was largely a propulsion literature**, because a single engine that could drive proprotors in hover and produce jet thrust in cruise was what the concept was thought to need. **DARPA was in it from the start.** A DARPA and National Aeronautics and Space Administration programme to demonstrate a convertible turbofan-turboshaft engine began on 13 May 1981, using a modified TF34-GE-400, for an engine able to power a rotorcraft "in vertical flight and in horizontal flight up to approximately .85 Mach number" \[[Bellin and Brooks 1983][research_bellin_brooks_1983]\]. **A study of the same period found that the fold tilt rotor needed a convertible engine giving thrust to Mach 0.75 and shaft power to proprotors in hover**, and identified a torque converter as the coupling that would let the fan be engaged and disengaged smoothly \[[Gill and Sauer 1983][research_gill_sauer_1983]\].

**The engine was built and run.** A report of 1988 describes a convertible engine with variable inlet guide vanes that ran stably and smoothly in turbofan, turboshaft and dual modes, the last combining fan and shaft power, with fuel consumption in turboshaft mode higher than a dedicated turboshaft's because of fan-tip churning \[[McArdle 1988a][research_mcardle_1988]\]. **Its conclusion bears most directly on the X-76.** Its revised mission analyses for a 400-knot rotorcraft concluded that convertible engines, rather than separate lift and cruise engines, would give a smaller, lighter craft with lower fuel use and lower direct operating cost.

**The X-76 uses separate lift and cruise engines, the configuration that analysis judged heavier.** The solicitation explains why, as far as a document can. It required the demonstrator to "be based on existing engine(s)/propulsion system", allowed only minor upgrades without core changes, and gave its reason, "to ensure the engine or propulsion system development does not delay the overall X-Plane flight demonstration" \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. **No convertible engine of this class is in production in any record read here, so the rule excluded the configuration the earlier literature preferred.** **The competitor's documents support this reading.** Aurora's Phase 1B design was a fan-in-wing aircraft, a configuration unlike Bell's in every structural respect, and it too carried "off-the-shelf turbofan and turboshaft engines" \[[Aurora on its SPRINT design, October 2024][ref_aurora_oct24]\], so both finalists answered the rule the same way. The engine mass fraction derived above is the price, and the solicitation accepted it for schedule. That causal reading is this article's inference, and the solicitation also states that the operational system "may include an engine/propulsion system that is envisioned in the future", which leaves the convertible engine open for the aircraft the X-76 is meant to inform.

### Folding Tiltrotor Demonstrators Were Proposed in 1985 and 1986

**A folding tiltrotor demonstrator was proposed twice in the mid-1980s and never built.** Gleiter's 1985 paper argued that the folding tiltrotor offered advantages "for missions requiring long endurance combined with a speed capability in excess of 400 knots", reported that development had begun in 1967 with "no significant technical obstacles", and proposed a demonstrator on either the V-22 or the S-3A powered by the convertible CTFS-34 engine \[[Gleiter 1985][research_gleiter_1985]\]. **A study a year later at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration considered three demonstrator candidates**, the V-22 with a convertible TF34, a modified S-3A with the same engines, and the XV-15 with a conceptual turbofan coupled through a torque converter \[[Eisenberg and Bowles 1986][research_eisenberg_bowles_1986]\]. **Every one of those proposals depended on a convertible engine.** The X-76 is the first folding tiltrotor demonstrator in the records read here to be funded through to manufacture, and it is being built without one \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\] \[[DARPA on the X-76][ref_darpa_x76]\].

### DARPA Paid for a Stop-Fold Study in 2008

**The federal award record holds a DARPA contract titled `STOP FOLD TILT ROTOR STUDY`**, awarded on 30 May 2008 to the Bell Boeing Joint Project Office for 584,557.50 dollars on a cost-sharing basis, extended at no cost to 31 March 2009, with one offer received \[[Award HR001108C0077 for a stop fold tilt rotor study][ref_award_stopfold_2008]\]. **No report from that study was found.** It sits between the 1980s demonstrator proposals and Bell's earliest stop-fold patent filings, and it shows that the agency now sponsoring the X-76 had paid for the configuration's study almost fifteen years before its solicitation.

**Bell's patent record dates the company's sustained work.** The earliest Bell filing found on in-flight blade folding has a priority date of 15 June 2010 and describes a foldable rotor system with a blade fold actuator and a swashplate that changes blade pitch \[[CA 2802389][ref_pat_ca2802389]\]. **A cluster of filings with a priority date of 2 December 2014 describes the transition mechanism itself**, a gimbal lock that enables and disables the rotor's gimballing freedom and a blade stop assembly whose arms extend in non-rotary flight \[[US 10,526,068][ref_pat_us10526068]\], a cam that locks the gimbal and the blade cuff together \[[US 10,336,447][ref_pat_us10336447]\], and a fold mechanism driven through the swashplate and pitch links \[[US 11,235,858][ref_pat_us11235858]\]. **The dates are consistent with Bell's July 2025 release, in which its engineering vice president calls the stop-fold aircraft an achievement Bell had been working towards for over 10 years** \[[Bell to build the SPRINT X-plane][ref_bell_phase2]\].

## Dependent Systems

**Every subsystem below is described from a certificate, a solicitation, a patent or a contractor's paper, and none from a description of the X-76 itself**, because none is public.

### The Turboshafts

**The CT7-8 was approved by the Federal Aviation Administration on 29 September 2000 under type certificate E8NE** \[[New Zealand type acceptance report for the CT7 series][ref_nz_ct7]\], General Electric announcing the certificate on 10 October 2000 for an engine selected for the 25,000-pound-class Sikorsky S-92 \[[General Electric on the CT7-8 certificate, 2000][ref_ge_ct7_2000]\]. **The European Union Aviation Safety Agency's data sheet gives its certification date as 20 January 2003**, a date taken over from a national approval that preceded the agency, with its basis in that American certificate, and the data sheet gives its output shaft speed as 21,945 revolutions per minute at its principal ratings \[[Type-certificate data sheet for the CT7 series][ref_easa_ct7]\]. **That speed fixes the size of the reduction the drive system must make**, since a proprotor of radius $r$ turning at tip speed $V\_t$ runs at

$$
N_r = \frac{60\, V_t}{2 \pi r}, \qquad \mathcal{G} = \frac{N_e}{N_r} = \frac{2 \pi r\, N_e}{60\, V_t}.
\tag{39}
$$

At the XV-15's own rotor speeds the reduction would be 37.3 in hover and 42.4 in airplane mode. **For a 15,000 pound X-76 at the XV-15's hover tip speed of 235 metres per second**, the rotor radii of the hover table give a proprotor speed of 547 revolutions per minute and a reduction of 40.1 at the XV-15's disk loading, 674 and 32.6 at a disk loading of 20, and 1,167 and 18.8 at a disk loading of 60. **A small stowable rotor needs a smaller reduction, a weight saving in the gearbox that partly offsets the weight of the fold**, and like every statement here about the X-76's rotor it depends on a disk loading that is not public. **The data sheet read is issue 10, dated 19 December 2025, four days after the article's date**, and the base model's ratings and mass quoted here are those of that issue. **A turboshaft of this family is a natural choice for the solicitation's existing-engine rule**, being the commercial counterpart of the T700 engines, which with the CT7 power 20 of the 47 rows whose basic mission symbol is H in the copy of the register last updated on 23 August 2026. **Whether the X-76's two turboshafts run in cruise, idle, or shut down is not public**, and the answer matters for fuel, for restart reliability before the rotors are unfolded, and for the thermal management system the budget book names.

### The Turbofan, and a Certificate That Requires Two of It

**The PW308C's primary certificate is Transport Canada's E-31**, which the New Zealand regulator validated on 18 October 2007 \[[New Zealand type acceptance report for the PW308 series][ref_nz_pw308]\], and the European data sheet read here is that agency's validation. **That sheet states that "the PW308A and PW308C engines are approved for multiple engine installation only"** \[[Type-certificate data sheet for the PW308 series][ref_easa_pw308]\]. It also records that the PW308C is normally used at a reduced take-off thrust of 3,113 decanewtons with an automatic increase to its full rating if the other engine fails. **Both are features of a certificate written for a twin-engine business jet.** If the X-76 carries one PW308C, as the register cell read literally and the renderings suggest, **its installation lies outside an assumption underlying the civil certificate.** The mismatch is not a defect, because the X-76 is an experimental aircraft flown under a DARPA flight release and not a civil type, and DARPA told proposers that engine certification "whether commercial or military does not matter as long as certification documents are available to substantiate whatever airworthiness method is chosen" \[[SPRINT questions and answers][ref_sprint_qa]\]. **But it means the engine's certification basis does not cover its installation, and whatever the civil certificate takes for granted about a second engine has to be substantiated another way.** This reading is inferred from the data sheet and the cell, and no document consulted states the number of turbofans fitted.

### The Drive System in Bell's Patents

**The budget book's subsystem list names a propulsion system, a thermal management system, hydraulics and an electrical system, and no drive system** \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2026][ref_darpa_pb2026]\]. **Bell's patents describe several.** One couples one or more rotor systems and one or more thrust fans through a combined gearbox with clutches, so that rotors and fans can be engaged in sequence through the transition \[[US 11,577,831][ref_pat_us11577831]\]. One lets a normally idle lift engine drive a pylon-mounted ducted fan for extra thrust once the blades are folded \[[US 11,325,719][ref_pat_us11325719]\]. One routes drive shafts through the wing to the rotor on the pylon \[[US 2023/0331393][ref_pat_us20230331393]\]. **A patent describes an embodiment and claims a right, and it does not say what was built.** **Whether the X-76 has a drive system of any of these kinds is not public.**

### The Fold Mechanism

**The transition has more locked states than a conventional tiltrotor has**, and Bell's filings describe each lock. A rotor-blade assembly in a 2023 filing has "a lock system to enable and disable a folding degree of freedom and a pitching degree of freedom" \[[US 2025/0100674][ref_pat_us20250100674]\], and a companion filing describes a blade position control system that selectively restricts pitch and fold through a multilobe component moved by an actuator \[[US 2025/0100680][ref_pat_us20250100680]\]. **A 2018 method folds the blades of a tiltrotor from an inverted-Y rotor position**, unlocking and restraining each blade in turn \[[US 10,858,094][ref_pat_us10858094]\], and a 2019 filing clamps the stowed blade pneumatically along the pylon \[[US 2021/0078695][ref_pat_us20210078695]\]. **A 2020 filing shapes the blade tip to cut drag when folded** \[[US 11,643,195][ref_pat_us11643195]\], and a 2020 filing applies the stop-fold rotor to a tail-sitter instead of a tiltrotor \[[US 2021/0253239][ref_pat_us20210253239]\]. **Taken together the filings show a decade of work on the locks, the stow and the folded drag**, which are the three things the 1972 test showed were possible and did not make light.

### Control Through Conversion

**The solicitation's flight test checkouts require the transition in both directions to be controlled at maximum design gross weight**, with handling qualities to Level 1 desired and Level 2 required by the military flying qualities handbook and hover manoeuvres judged against the rotorcraft handling qualities specification's mission task elements \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\], those being MIL-HDBK-1797 \[[MIL-HDBK-1797, Flying Qualities of Piloted Aircraft][ref_mil_hdbk_1797]\] and ADS-33E-PRF \[[ADS-33E-PRF, Handling Qualities Requirements for Military Rotorcraft][ref_ads_33e]\]. **The slides write the latter as "ADS-PRF-33"**, which this article reads as the same Army specification. The airworthiness basis is MIL-HDBK-516C \[[MIL-HDBK-516C, Airworthiness Certification Criteria][ref_mil_hdbk_516c]\]. **Bell's paper on the sled test describes fly-by-wire transition controls that automatically manage each step of the transition from proprotor flight to jet flight and back** \[[Schank et al. 2025][research_schank_xin_2025]\]. **The conversion of a stop-fold aircraft is a sequence of discrete events**, feathering, stopping, indexing, locking and folding, and its reverse, each of which changes the aircraft's mass distribution and drag. Such a sequence is a control problem for software and not for a pilot's hands, which is consistent with an uncrewed demonstrator, as an inference.

**The structural guidance is modest because the demonstrator is not a fighter.** The solicitation asks for load margins from minus 0.5 to plus 2 g, a 500-hour design life, and a 12 feet per second sink rate at landing without damage \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\]. **The fiscal year 2027 book adds a structural proof load test to verify that the built aircraft matches its structural design predictions** \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2027][ref_darpa_pb2027]\], a plan published after the dateline.

## The Contractor Overstates Bell's Designation History

**Bell's March 2026 release claims that the company "has pushed the known boundaries of flight through pioneering high speed and vertical lift aircraft from the X-1 to the XV-3 and XV-15"** \[[Bell on the X-76][ref_bell_x76]\], and its Phase 1A release of November 2023 called the X-1 and the XV-15 "memorable X-planes" \[[Bell selected for SPRINT Phase 1A][ref_bell_phase1a]\]. **The XV-3 and XV-15 are not research designations.** They belong to the convertiplane sequence, mission letter V with the experimental status prefix X, and the designating instruction states that a design number "identifies major design changes within the same basic mission" and stands to the right of "the basic mission or vehicle type symbols" \[[Department of the Air Force Instruction 16-401, 2020][ref_dafi_16_401_2020]\]. **Under that rule, which the [X-67][related_post_a364_x67_slot_taken_by_xq67] article examined, the V sequence is a different count from the research series.** **Bell's research designations are eight**, the [X-1][related_post_a298_bell_x1], [X-2][related_post_a299_bell_x2], [X-5][related_post_a302_bell_x5], [X-9][related_post_a306_bell_x9], [X-14][related_post_a311_bell_x14], [X-16][related_post_a313_bell_x16], [X-22][related_post_a319_bell_x22] and now the X-76. **The X-76 is Bell's first research designation since the X-22**, and its only research designation for a rotorcraft that converts by stopping its rotors \[[Wikipedia, List of X-planes][ref_wiki_list_of_x_planes]\]. The releases' framing is a heritage claim, and on its own terms a fair one, since the XV-3 made the first full in-flight conversion from helicopter to airplane mode on 18 December 1958 \[[The History of the XV-15 Tilt Rotor Research Aircraft][ref_xv15_history]\]. **It is recorded here only because it uses X-plane for a designation the series does not count.**

## The Flight Test Record Is Empty

**Nothing has flown.** At the article's date Bell had been selected for Phase 2, which the solicitation placed after a preliminary design review, the fiscal year 2026 plans placed the programme in critical design, and a DARPA spokesperson had told the press that the agency expected a completed demonstrator in 2027 and flight testing in 2028 \[[Breaking Defense on the Phase 2 selection][ref_bd_phase2]\].

### The Sled Test and the Wind Tunnel Are Ground Tests

**Bell's two risk reduction tests are the only test data the programme has reported, and both are ground tests.** In late 2023 a track-guided test vehicle ran on the 10-mile High Speed Test Track at Holloman Air Force Base, integrating "multi-mode propulsion, folding proprotors, and fly-by-wire transition controls" \[[Schank et al. 2025][research_schank_xin_2025]\] \[[Bell awarded funding for SPRINT Phase 1B][ref_bell_phase1b]\]. **Bell's paper on it claims "the first known powered prop-to-jet and jet-to-prop transition"**, a narrower and more defensible claim than first-ever stop-fold technology, since the 1972 test stopped and folded a rotor in a tunnel but did not carry a whole powered vehicle through the transition. In 2024 a wind tunnel programme at the National Institute for Aviation Research at Wichita State University "validated the stability and control of the aircraft through the rotor fold and unfold sequence in flight" \[[Bell completes stop-fold wind tunnel testing][ref_bell_windtunnel]\], the release being dated 4 December 2024. **Neither result is published in numbers in any document consulted.**

## Comparison With Ground Prediction

**There is no flight result to set beside any ground prediction, because the X-76 had not flown by 15 December 2025.** What the record holds is prediction of three kinds. The first is the government's specification, which asks for at least 400 knots true airspeed between 15,000 and 30,000 feet, a gross take-off weight of 8,000 to 15,000 pounds, and hover out of ground effect at 4,000 feet on a 95 degree Fahrenheit day \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\]. The second is the contractor's ground testing, the sled run at Holloman Air Force Base and the wind tunnel programme at Wichita State University, described above and not reported in numbers. The third is this article's derivation from certificated engine ratings and the solicitation's envelope, set out in Sizing From First Principles.

**The nearest thing to a comparison of prediction with result is historical, and it was made on the ground.** Engle and Sambell placed rotor stopping in the 120 to 200 knot speed range in 1969 \[[Engle and Sambell 1969][research_engle_sambell_1969]\], and the full-scale folding rotor tested in 1972 was stopped and started at tunnel speeds up to 175 knots \[[Large Scale Wind Tunnel 1972][research_reportcr114464_1972]\], inside that range. **Both are analytical or wind tunnel results, and neither involved a whole aircraft in flight.** Bell's sled test carried a powered vehicle through the transition on rails \[[Schank et al. 2025][research_schank_xin_2025]\], a step closer to flight and still a ground test.

**The predictions this article makes are stated so that flight could check them.** They are a drag-area ceiling of 0.60 to 0.84 square metres at 400 knots, from the relation for $f\_{\max}$, a heaviest hover weight of about 30,800 pounds at sea level at the XV-15's disk loading, from the relation for $W\_{\max}$, and a conversion band bounded by illustrative stall speeds of 105 to 136 knots, from the stall relation, and by the 175 to 200 knots of the historical tests. **Each depends on assumptions listed under Where the Framing Breaks Down, and none has been tested against the aircraft.** The fiscal year 2027 budget book plans a structural proof load test to verify that the built aircraft matches its structural design predictions \[[DARPA budget justification, fiscal year 2027][ref_darpa_pb2027]\], which postdates the article and is itself a ground test. The comparisons a first flight would make possible follow.

### What Would Be Compared With What

**When the X-76 flies, four of this article's derivations become testable.** Its hover gross weight and rotor diameter fix its disk loading, which can be set against the hover envelope above. Its demonstrated cruise speed and altitude, with its weight, fix a required lift-to-drag ratio, and its level-flight thrust setting, if published, fixes its equivalent drag area against the ceiling of 0.60 to 0.84 square metres at 400 knots that the relation for $f\_{\max}$ gives. **Its conversion speed can be set against the band from wing stall to between 175 and 200 knots** that the historical tests and the stall relation together suggest. **And its maximum demonstrated speed can be set against the solicitation's threshold of 400 and objective of 450 knots**, the gap between which is the gap between a proprotor that must be slowed and one that must be stopped.

## What the Data Changed Awaits a First Flight

**If the X-76 meets its threshold, the first thing it settles is not speed but the conversion.** That a proprotor aircraft can hover and that a jet can push a clean airframe to 400 knots are both established separately. **No record consulted shows the sequence between them in flight**, with a real wing, a real jet, and blades being stopped and folded in a real airstream at the low end of the conversion band, where the stopped-blade instabilities of the 1960s tests were found. **A clean conversion in both directions would retire the risk that shelved the concept in 1972 other than the convertible engine**, and the convertible engine would then become the remaining argument for the operational aircraft.

**If it meets the objective of 450 knots, it would show that the folded configuration is clean enough to fit the drag budget a single business-jet turbofan sets**, 0.47 to 0.66 square metres of equivalent drag area at 450 knots by the relation for $f\_{\max}$, the article's quantitative claim about the configuration and the one most sensitive to how well the folded blades are faired.

**What it may fail to influence is the procurement it is meant to inform.** The budget books' transition partner moved from service members to services to a component, and **Special Operations Command, the joint partner on every DARPA page, is named as transition partner in none of them.** The literature records two folding tiltrotor demonstrators proposed in the 1980s and neither built, and the configuration's history is one of feasibility repeatedly shown and repeatedly not bought. **The X-76 changes that history only if someone buys what it demonstrates**, a decision no flight test makes.

## The Contemporary Literature

| Cluster | Records |
|---|---|
| Stopped, folded and stowed rotors | 93 |
| The tiltrotor and its relatives | 1,198 |
| Proprotor whirl flutter and tiltrotor aeroelasticity | 130 |
| High-speed propellers and tip compressibility | 191 |
| High-speed vertical lift as a class | 882 |
| Hover, wake, downwash and the surface | 277 |
| Conversion between hover and forward flight | 42 |
| Turboshafts, turbofans and the convertible engine | 383 |
| Rotorcraft conceptual design and sizing | 73 |
| The missions the solicitation names | 44 |
| Research aircraft and their flight test | 99 |
| **Total** | **3,412** |

**There is almost no literature on the X-76 itself, and the one paper on its direct ancestor is the contractor's.** Bell's 2025 paper on the stop-fold sled test is the only technical publication in the survey about the programme's hardware \[[Schank et al. 2025][research_schank_xin_2025]\]. **What the survey maps is the large literature the X-76 sits in**, being the stopped and folding rotor, the tiltrotor and its aeroelastic and compressibility limits, high-speed vertical lift as a class, hover physics and the downwash at the surface, conversion between modes, the propulsion families and the convertible engine, rotorcraft conceptual design, the missions the solicitation names, and the practice of research aircraft and their flight test.

**The survey cites 3,412 research records**, 17 of them the research primaries described in The Source Base and 3,395 drawn from a bibliographic index of the journal and conference literature and from the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's reports server. Each record appears in one cluster only. **714 of them, 20.9 percent, are report primaries** under the identifier rule set out under The Definition of Primary, and the 3,371 records that carry a year run from 1949 to 2027 with a median of 2007.

**The clusters are uneven and the unevenness is informative.** The tiltrotor literature is the largest and the conversion literature the smallest. **The configuration the X-76 embodies has a literature with a gap in the middle.** Of the 50 titles in the survey that name a folded, folding, stopped or stowed rotor, blade or propeller, 35 date from 1965 to 1999, none from the 2000s, and 15 from 2010 on, 10 of them from 2021 on. Titles that join a folded or stowed rotor to a tiltrotor or proprotor number 15, 14 of them from 1969 to 1992, a span that holds the convertible engine programmes and the V-22's blade fold for stowage, and one from 2011, and the stopped-rotor revival of the 2020s is led by the high-speed vertical take-off and landing work this programme belongs to \[[Young 2024][research_young_2024]\].

### What the Literature Establishes, and Where It Is Moving

**Read as a whole rather than cluster by cluster, the literature makes four points that bear on the X-76, and it is silent on a fifth.**

**First, the stopped rotor has an experimental base from the 1960s and 1970s and a revival in the 2020s, and the revival is divided.** The early work found that a stopped blade can go violently unstable at some combinations of shaft and pitch angle \[[White 1969][research_white_1969]\], and that a full-scale folding proprotor could be stopped and started in about two seconds \[[Large Scale Wind Tunnel 1972][research_reportcr114464_1972]\]. **The contemporary reassessment by Brown and Ahuja reviews why the historical stopped-rotor experiments were not successful and argues that "with modern technologies, materials, and analysis tools" a low disc-loading rotor can be used "not only for efficient VTOL but also for efficient cruise"** \[[Brown and Ahuja 2023a][research_brown_ahuja_2023]\], where VTOL is vertical take-off and landing. Young's survey of novel concepts for flight at 400 knots or more, written at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, discusses "two stopped-rotor concepts and two non-stopped-rotor concepts" \[[Young 2024][research_young_2024]\]. **So the current literature splits between keeping the stopped rotor in the airstream as a lifting surface and removing it from the airstream altogether**, and the X-76 belongs to the second branch, as the contractor's sled-test paper states \[[Schank et al. 2025][research_schank_xin_2025]\]. Work on the flight dynamics of stopped-rotor aircraft continues at small scale, judging by one paper's title \[[He et al. 2022][research_he_gao_2022]\].

**Second, whirl flutter is a large and recent experimental subject, and every result cited here is about making a turning proprotor survive at higher speed.** Of the 209 titles in the survey that name whirl flutter, 105 are dated 2020 or later. The Maryland Tiltrotor Rig is a Froude-scaled, 4.75-foot, semispan flutter rig first tested to 100 knots in the Navy's Carderock tunnel \[[Tsai et al. 2024][research_tsai_sutherland_2024]\]. Its swept-tip blades, swept 20 degrees aft from 80 percent of radius, showed "higher wing chord damping using swept-tip blades in freewheel conditions" \[[Sutherland et al. 2024][research_sutherland_tsai_2024]\], and the comprehensive analysis matched wing beam damping well while underpredicting chord damping and missing the effect of powered operation \[[Gul and Datta 2024][research_gul_datta_2024]\]. **Run to 200 knots in freewheeling airplane mode, the model "remained flutter-free up to 200 knots", but its "chord damping showed signs of a sudden drop after 175 knots"** \[[Akinwale and Datta 2023][research_akinwale_datta_2023]\], and a 2026 analysis of the same rig's free decays found that damping falls with response amplitude, "a trend missed by conventional linear estimation methods" \[[Simmons and Riso 2026][research_simmons_riso_2026]\]. **The European Advanced Testbed for Tiltrotor Aeroelastics, called ATTILA, a Froude-scale semispan model of a civil tiltrotor's wing and proprotor, found the wing torsion mode "displaying a sharp trend towards negative damping at higher speeds"** and an unexpected contribution from stiction in the blade pitch mechanism \[[van 't Hoff et al 2024][research_vanthoff_kapteijn_2024]\], which a 2026 analysis could reproduce only by modelling friction in the joints \[[De Vita et al. 2026][research_devita_cassoni_2026]\]. **A design study found that replacing one large wingtip rotor with two of half the disk area "pushed the instability speed by more than 100%"** \[[Gul and Yeo 2025][research_gul_yeo_2025]\]. The standing reviews are Reed's of 1965 \[[Reed 1965][research_reed_1965]\] and Kunz's of 2002 and 2005 \[[Kunz 2002][research_kunz_2002]\] \[[Kunz 2005][research_kunz_2005]\], the latter cited for their titles. **This literature is the measure of what the X-76 avoids.** The stop-fold configuration's premise is that removing the rotor from the airstream is easier than making it stable there, and a body of current work in which a scaled rig is flutter-free to 200 knots but losing chord damping above 175 is the evidence for that premise. Scaled speeds do not transfer to full-scale speeds without the rig's scaling laws, and this article does not attempt the transfer.

**Third, the convertible engine, the missing piece of 1972, has had almost no new literature in the survey since the 1990s.** The DARPA and National Aeronautics and Space Administration programme of 1981 \[[Bellin and Brooks 1983][research_bellin_brooks_1983]\], the 1988 stand test and mission analysis \[[McArdle 1988a][research_mcardle_1988]\] and a 1996 report whose title concerns the engine's dynamic and transient performance \[[McArdle et al. 1996][research_mcardle_barth_1996]\] are the field's last substantial entries before a gap of more than twenty years. Of the 33 titles in the survey that name a convertible or turboshaft-turbofan engine, 31 date from 1967 to 1998, and the other two are from 2025 and 2026, on the performance and the mode-transition control of a turboshaft-turbofan engine \[[Jia et al. 2025b][research_jia_chen_2025]\] \[[Li et al. 2026][research_li_xie_2026]\]. **Both SPRINT finalists then answered the existing-engine rule with separate engines** \[[Aurora on its SPRINT design, October 2024][ref_aurora_oct24]\], so the current programme could not use the literature's preferred solution.

**Fourth, the hover side of runway independence rests on measurements that are decades old.** The full-scale tiltrotor hover data are the Ames tests of the 1980s \[[Felker et al. 1985][research_felker_betzina_1985]\] \[[Felker et al. 1986a][research_felker_maisel_1986]\], and a 2017 report set out to widen that experimental base because computational work had concentrated on only two successful tiltrotors, the XV-15 and the MV-22B \[[Harris 2017a][research_harris_2017]\]. The title of one study places it most directly on people standing in a rotor's outwash \[[Calvert and Wenren 2019][research_calvert_wenren_2019_2]\]. **The contemporary high-speed vertical take-off and landing design studies, including a 2024 preliminary design study and a student design competition winner, are cited for their titles** \[[Yang et al. 2024a][research_yang_coxgross_2024]\] \[[O'Brien and Delgado 2024][research_obrien_delgado_2024]\].

**And the literature is silent on the X-76's keystone.** No title in the survey reports a stop-fold conversion in flight. Bell's sled test is the only powered prop-to-jet transition of a whole vehicle in the survey, the first known by its authors' account, and it was on rails \[[Schank et al. 2025][research_schank_xin_2025]\]. **The X-76's flight test would fill that gap, and it lies after the dateline.**

### Stopped, folded and stowed rotors

**This is the X-76's own lineage.** It holds the rotor-stopping and stowed-rotor studies of the mid-1960s, the folding-proprotor studies of the late 1960s and 1970s, the full-scale folding rotor test of 1972, the stopped-rotor and rotor/wing concepts including the [X-50][related_post_a347_boeing_x50]'s canard rotor/wing, the X-wing's stopped-rotor dynamics, and the stopped-rotor revival of the 2020s.

### Conversion between hover and forward flight

**The keystone's own literature, and it is small.** It holds the jet, ducted-propeller and fan models tested in transition in the 1950s and 1960s, and since 2020 mostly the transition control of small unmanned aircraft. The conversion of tiltrotors and tilt-wings is in the tiltrotor cluster above.

**Of its 42 records, 20 are dated 2020 or later and 8 are dated 1969 or earlier**, and 24 titles name an unmanned, micro or drone vehicle, 15 of them from 2020 on. No title in it names a rotor that stops.

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The aircraft's mass is the unknown that every envelope here is drawn around.** The hover weights, the power fractions, the engine mass fraction and the required lift-to-drag ratio are all functions of a gross weight that is not public, and the inferences drawn from them about where the X-76 lies are inferences.

**The turbofan's lapse is assumed.** The drag-area ceiling is exact in its algebra and approximate in its input, since the factor $\varphi$ is swept rather than known, and a real turbofan's lapse is not a pure function of density. **The altitude independence of the ceiling is exactly as good as that assumption.**

**The hover assumptions are typical rather than measured.** A figure of merit of 0.75, a drive efficiency of 0.90 and a download of 10 percent are reasonable for a tiltrotor, and the X-76's proprotors, which must fold, may be less efficient in hover than an optimised proprotor. **The turboshafts' hot-day lapse is not modelled at all**, so every hot-day hover weight above is high by an unknown amount.

**The proprotor's speed limit is taken from compressibility alone.** Whirl flutter, which the historical record names as the reason the first stop-fold tests stopped the rotor, is cited and not computed \[[The History of the XV-15 Tilt Rotor Research Aircraft][ref_xv15_history]\], and for a particular aircraft it may bind at a lower speed than the helical tip Mach number does. **The 0.85 limit is an assumption.**

**The register's engine cell is the only configuration fact attributed to Department of Defense records**, its plus sign is unexplained, and the turbofan count of one is a reading. With $n\_F$ turbofans the drag ceiling is

$$
f_{\max} = \frac{2\, n_F\, F_0\, \varphi}{\rho_0 V^2},
\tag{40}
$$

**so if the X-76 carries two turbofans, the drag budget doubles and the certificate point disappears**, and no source this article found excludes that.

**And the patents describe embodiments of a company's work, not the X-76.** They are cited for what Bell has filed and for the problems those filings address, and no sentence here claims that any patented mechanism is fitted to the aircraft.

## The Source Base

**This article rests on a broad base of government primary documents, and almost all of them are about the programme rather than the aircraft.** The solicitation, its slides and its questions and answers were read from the contracting portal \[[SPRINT broad agency announcement][ref_sprint_baa]\] \[[SPRINT proposers day slides][ref_sprint_overview]\] \[[SPRINT questions and answers][ref_sprint_qa]\]. Four budget justification books were read in full for the programme's entries. **The award record was read by contract and by transaction**, with three first-phase contracts and the 2008 study found and Bell's instruments not found. **Aurora's two releases of 2024 were read for the competitor's propulsion and schedule.** The designating instruction of 2020 was read for its definition of a design number, and the three flight-standard documents the solicitation names were identified from their catalogue entries and not read. **DARPA's programme page was read at its current version and as archived on 24 December 2024, 12 May 2025, 10 July 2025 and 12 December 2025** \[[DARPA SPRINT programme page, as archived on 12 May 2025][ref_darpa_sprint_wb_2025_05]\] \[[DARPA SPRINT programme page, as archived on 10 July 2025][ref_darpa_sprint_wb_2025_07]\], the last three days before this article's date, and every statement about the programme as it stood at the date rests on that capture.

**Apart from DARPA's picture, the engine certification documents are the only primary documents about the aircraft's hardware.** They are the European Union Aviation Safety Agency's data sheets and the New Zealand regulator's two type acceptance reports, the latter dated 2007 and 2020 and so inside this article's date, read because the Federal Aviation Administration's and Transport Canada's own sheets were not retrieved, together with General Electric's certification releases of 2000 and 2004. **The New Zealand report on the PW308 gives its take-off rating in pounds and agrees with the European sheet's kilonewtons to within a pound**, which is the only cross-check of a rating this article could make between two regulators. DARPA's artist's concept of the X-76 was read as an image, and the reading is stated as a reading of a picture. **The register, whose compiler attributes every cell of the row but the description to Department of Defense records, is the only document naming the engines**, read at its current version and at the three archived copies that bracket the row's first appearance.

**Bell's releases were read from Bell's newsroom and, for two of them, from Textron's investor-relations mirror**, which carries the two wrong datelines described above. **Fourteen of Bell's patent publications were read for their abstracts** and are cited for nothing their abstracts do not say. **The National Aeronautics and Space Administration history of the XV-15 was read for its account of the 1972 folding rotor test, its appendix specifications and its chronology**, and seventeen research primaries were read for their abstracts, and one of them, the 1985 XV-15 rotor hover test, in part for its text.

**One document the article would most like to have read could not be.** Bell's Phase 1 and Phase 2 instruments, presumably other transactions, are not in the award record, so the value of the contract that is building the X-76 is not known to this article.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is a report primary when its address is on the National Aeronautics and Space Administration's Technical Reports Server or it carries a Defense Technical Information Center identifier, being an address at dtic.mil or a digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix. **Of the 3,412 research records, 714, or 20.9 percent, are report primaries under that rule**, most of them in the tiltrotor cluster, 284, and the high-speed vertical lift cluster, 237. **The rule reaches 8 of the 17 research primaries this article read for their abstracts**, among them the 1972 folding rotor test report, the Ames hover tests and the convertible engine stand test, and not the other 9, which are society and journal papers such as Engle and Sambell's of 1969 and Bell's of 2025, so 20.9 percent is a lower bound on how much of the survey is first-hand.

### Thin Subjects

**Six subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms, with a hyphen or a slash read as a space.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the thrust lapse of a turbofan with altitude and speed | thrust lapse, lapse rate, lapse | 0 |
| the helical tip Mach number of a propeller or proprotor | helical tip | 3 |
| the hover figure of merit | figure of merit, figures of merit | 2 |
| the conversion corridor | conversion corridor, conversion corridors, transition corridor, transition corridors | 7 |
| the weight of an engine | engine weight, engine mass, powerplant weight | 4 |
| restarting a turboshaft | restart, relight, airstart | 3 |

**No title names a turbofan's thrust lapse**, so the factor $\varphi$ of The Jet Is a Drag Budget is swept as an assumption because the literature gives the article nothing to take it from.

**The helical tip Mach number is a propeller acoustician's variable.** The 3 titles that name it are all on the noise of propellers and propfans, and none names a proprotor, so the speed limit of The Proprotor's Speed Limit Forces the Rotor to Stop applies a propeller variable to a proprotor.

**Two titles name a figure of merit, and neither names a tiltrotor or a proprotor**, so the hover table's figure of merit of 0.75 is an assumption in the literature's titles as well as in the text.

**The conversion corridor is named in 7 titles**, 6 of them on tiltrotors and tilt-wings and 1 on a short take-off and vertical landing propulsion system, and none on a rotor that stops and folds, so the conversion band derived above has no published counterpart for the stop-fold configuration.

**Four titles name the weight or mass of an engine, all of them turboshafts or rotorcraft powerplants, and none a turbofan**, so the engine mass fraction of The Engines Alone Are a Sixth of the Heaviest Aeroplane rests on certificated dry masses and not on a weight model.

**Three titles name a turboshaft restart, two of them sharing one title**, and all are about the engine on its own, so the restart before the rotors are unfolded that the section on dependent systems names is not a subject of any title.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject**, meaning that the title bears on a subject the argument above uses. **The subject's vocabulary is rich in homonyms, and the excluded classes show it.** T700 names a carbon fibre and a steel grade as well as a turboshaft family, propeller names the propellers of ships and outboard motors and molecular propellers, hover names a manoeuvre in wireless communication, flutter is also a disorder of the heart, and austere environments, brownout, outwash, convertible and conversion corridor belong also to medicine, power grids, glaciology, finance and land use. Rotor wing also means a helicopter in the literature of medical transport, a rotor wake is also the wake of a compressor or fan rotor, and the vertical take-off and landing aircraft of nonlinear control theory is a planar benchmark model and not an aircraft. **Titles that apply the subject to something the argument does not use are excluded too**, such as cabin and interior noise, icing, crashworthiness and escape, avionics and cockpit displays, radar and infrared signatures, batteries, fuels and emissions, maintenance, air traffic and vertiport operations, and the path planning of small unmanned aircraft. Correction, erratum and withdrawal notices, news items, book reviews, supplementary video files, and dictionary and encyclopedia entries of two pages or fewer are excluded because they are not research works.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** The downwash of agricultural spraying aircraft and the sediment entrained by a rotor's downwash are kept because their subject is the flow below a rotor, turboshafts in ships and heavy equipment because their subject is the engine, a stopped-rotor concept for Venus because it is a stopped rotor, histories and procurement studies of the V-22 and of Future Vertical Lift because this article discusses procurement, and control displays and airspeed sensors for vertical take-off and landing aircraft because they bear on handling qualities. A reader may weigh each accordingly. **No cluster is a residual**, since each is named for a subject the argument uses.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.** A reading of titles cannot show that a work is relevant in substance, so this is a statement about titles only.

## Epistemic State

### The Article's Own Vantage Point

**The article is dated 15 December 2025 and written on 2 October 2026.** The allocation of the designation happened inside its dateline, 56 days before it. **The designation's publication did not**, the register first showing the row between 15 January and 1 February 2026 and DARPA announcing it on 9 March 2026. Everything this article reports about the programme from government documents of March 2023 through June 2025 was public at its date. **Everything it reports about the aircraft's name, critical design review and current schedule was not.**

### Historical Fact, From Primary Documents

- The X-76A was allocated on 20 October 2025 to Bell Textron, sponsor DARPA, with the engine cell `2 GE CT7-8, PW308C+` and a description marked as the compiler's.
- DARPA posted solicitation HR001123S0031 in March 2023 with the demonstrator guidance, mission and engine rule as quoted, a 42-month goal to first flight, and a Phase 1 budget of 75 million dollars.
- Three first-phase contracts are in the award record with the dates, values and offer count stated, and a 2008 DARPA stop-fold tilt rotor study to the Bell Boeing Joint Project Office is too.
- The budget books carry the figures, wording and plans as tabulated and quoted.
- The CT7-8 and PW308C ratings and masses are as their data sheets state, and the PW308C is approved for multiple-engine installation only.
- A folding 25-foot proprotor was stopped and started more than forty times in a full-scale wind tunnel test in 1972, and the concept was then set aside for weight, complexity and the lack of a developed convertible engine.
- DARPA and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration funded a convertible turbofan-turboshaft engine programme beginning on 13 May 1981.
- Both Phase 1B designs carried existing turbofan and turboshaft engines, Aurora's by its own release of October 2024.
- The CT7-8 was approved by the Federal Aviation Administration on 29 September 2000, and the PW308C's primary certificate is Transport Canada's E-31.

### Measured From the Documents Rather Than Asserted by Them

- The row's first public appearance, between 15 January and 1 February 2026, by archive capture.
- The absence of any Bell instrument from the award record under the searches described.
- The three-month disagreement among DARPA's and Bell's statements on when Phase 2 began.
- The one-year dateline errors on Textron's mirror of two releases.
- The count of 23 other register rows powered by T700 or CT7 engines and the absence of any other turboshaft and turbofan pairing, in the copy of the register last updated on 23 August 2026.

### Engineering Analysis, Derived Here and Checkable

- The hover envelope of two CT7-8s across disk loading, at the stated figure of merit, drive efficiency and download.
- The drag-area ceiling $f\_{\max} = 2 F\_0 \varphi / (\rho\_0 V^2)$ and its independence of altitude under the stated lapse model.
- The required lift-to-drag ratios across the solicitation's weight and altitude bands.
- The helical tip Mach numbers at the XV-15's tip speed and the tip speed reductions needed to hold 0.85.
- The engine mass fractions of 0.163 and 0.306 at the solicitation's weight limits.
- The schedule slip of at least eight months against the solicitation's goal.

### Inference, Stated as Such

- That the X-76 is heavier than 15,000 pounds or near it, from the engine mass fraction alone, since the hover power margin admits a heavier aircraft, a large margin or a high disk loading and does not choose between them.
- That it hovers at a disk loading well above a conventional tiltrotor's, from the stowed-blade geometry and the absence of a disk loading limit.
- That it carries one turbofan, from the register cell read literally and the renderings.
- That it is uncrewed, from the compiler's description, the solicitation's flight termination clause and the budget book's ground station.
- That Bell's instruments are other transactions, from the solicitation's permission and the award record's silence.
- That the existing-engine rule is why the X-76 has separate lift and cruise engines rather than the convertible engine the earlier literature preferred, a reading the competitor's identical choice supports.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**What the plus sign after the turbofan means.** How many turbofans are fitted. The aircraft's gross weight, rotor diameter, wing area and drag. Whether the turboshafts run in cruise. **Whether any patented drive or fold mechanism is fitted.** The value of Bell's contract. **And the keystone itself, since no stop-fold aircraft has converted in flight in any record read here.**

### Statements in This Article That Postdate Its Own Date

- The register's publication of the X-76A row, between 15 January and 1 February 2026.
- DARPA's and Bell's announcements of 9 March 2026, with the designation, the critical design review, the programme manager's rank, the 1776 statement and the plan for flight testing in early 2028.
- DARPA's programme page in its current form, and DARPA's artist's concept of the X-76, whose single exhaust and absent cockpit glazing are read here.
- The fiscal year 2027 budget book of April 2026, its figures for fiscal years 2025 through 2027, and its plans, each marked where used.
- The CT7 data sheet's issue 10, dated 19 December 2025, four days after the date, whose base-model ratings are used.
- The defence journalism of March 2026 \[[Air and Space Forces on the X-76][ref_afa_x76]\] \[[The War Zone on the X-76][ref_twz_x76]\] \[[The Aviationist on the X-76][ref_aviationist_x76]\].
- **The award record, read in October 2026**, whose totals include modifications through August 2025 and are therefore current totals rather than totals as they stood at any one earlier date.
- The literature survey, drawn from current indexes and including records dated to 2026 and one dated to 2027 by its publisher's metadata.

## Out of Scope

**The designation's number.** Why this aircraft is the X-76 and not the X-69 is the [X-69 through X-75][related_post_a366_x69_through_x75_leapfrogged_block] article's subject and is not reargued here.

**The operational aircraft.** The solicitation's operational system, its 5,000 pound payload and its cargo bay are described because they bound the demonstrator, and the operational aircraft's sizing, which would need a mission fuel analysis, is not attempted.

**Aeroelastic analysis.** Whirl flutter and the stopped-blade instabilities are cited as the reasons the configuration exists and as risks to its conversion, and neither is computed, since both need structural properties that are not public.

**Acoustics and signatures.** The literature on tiltrotor noise is in the survey because it is part of the tiltrotor's literature, and the X-76's acoustic or other signatures are not treated.

**The competing configurations.** Aurora's Phase 1 design is described here only for its propulsion and schedule, from Aurora's releases, and the Phase 1A designs of Northrop Grumman and Piasecki are not described in any primary document read here. The comparative literature on high-speed rotorcraft concepts is cited without being used to rank them.

**The procurement that would follow**, a question about the services' budgets rather than about an aeroplane.

## Conclusion

**The X-76 is a demonstrator built to answer one question, whether an aircraft can hover over an unprepared surface and then cruise at 400 knots or more, and its answer is to carry two propulsion systems and use them one at a time.** Two CT7-8 turboshafts lift it on proprotors, a PW308C turbofan pushes it once those proprotors have been stopped and folded, and the register's engine cell, the only configuration fact in the public record attributed to Department of Defense records, says so in one short line that ends in an unexplained plus sign.

**The certificated ratings of those engines bound the aircraft from both ends without its mass**, through the relations derived in Sizing From First Principles. At the assumed hover efficiencies, the turboshafts' 3,758 kilowatts would hover about 30,800 pounds at the XV-15's disk loading, twice the solicitation's heaviest guidance, so either the X-76 is heavier than its guidance, or it hovers with a large margin, or its proprotors are small and its disk loading high. **The turbofan's sea-level thrust fixes the largest equivalent drag area the aircraft can carry at 400 knots, 0.60 to 0.84 square metres across the assumed lapse, and the density cancels, so that ceiling is the same at every altitude in the solicitation's band.** The folded configuration has to fit inside it. **And the engines alone are a sixth of the solicitation's heaviest aircraft**, which is the price of carrying two systems.

**The concept is at least sixty years old in the open literature and was shown at full scale in a wind tunnel in 1972**, when a folding 25-foot proprotor was stopped and started more than forty times. It was then set aside for its weight, its complexity, and the lack of a convertible engine that could drive rotors and make jet thrust in one machine. **The 1980s built that engine and proposed folding tiltrotor demonstrators around it, and none was built.** The X-76 accepts the weight and the complexity and goes around the engine, because its solicitation required existing engines so that engine development could not delay first flight. **The earlier literature judged separate lift and cruise engines the heavier choice, and the X-76 makes it anyway.** The solicitation's existing-engine rule explains why, and the competing finalist's identical choice, a turbofan and a turboshaft in a fan-in-wing aircraft, supports the reading that the rule and not the configuration drove it.

**On 15 December 2025 nothing had flown, the designation was not public, and the schedule had moved by at least eight months against the solicitation's goal.** The programme's documents disagree on when its second phase began, a contractor's mirror misdates two of its releases by a year, and the contract that is building the aircraft was not found in the public award record. **The question the X-76 exists to answer, the conversion, remains open**, because hovering and fast cruise have each been done and the sequence between them, in flight, with a real wing and a real jet, has not.
